reports.games: Hearts of Iron IV (Paradox, 2016; patches through No Step Back 1.11 and Götterdämmerung 1.15 special-projects era)

systems.how_it_works: All building is done by civilian factories assigned to a national construction queue. Each civ factory contributes 5 build-points/day to its assigned project; max 15 factories per project (75/day cap per site). Construction speed is multiplied by stacking national modifiers (economy law, Construction I-V tech at +10% each, advisors, focus spirits — 75%+ total is routine) and then by local infrastructure: speed ×(1 + 0.1×infra level). Civ factories used for construction are the same pool used for consumer goods (a percentage tax set by economy law) and trade. Buildings cost fixed totals: civ factory 10,800 points, mil factory 7,200, infrastructure 6,000, refinery 14,500. Each state has a building-slot cap by state category, expandable via tech/laws.
systems.strengths: One fungible currency (civ factories) makes every construction decision a clean opportunity-cost question: build vs trade vs consumer goods. The queue with drag-priority is legible and low-micro. Infrastructure-as-local-multiplier creates a real 'develop the region first?' decision. Fixed per-site throughput caps stop instant mega-projects.
systems.weaknesses: Because civs build more civs, the optimal opening for every major is near-identical (pure civ spam until ~18-24 months before war, then flip to mils) — the infamous civ snowball; a civ factory pays itself back in ~2-3 years, so the decision is a solved compound-interest problem, not a strategic one. Construction has no labor, materials, or regional constraint — a factory in Berlin builds a port in Borneo. Infra-before-factories 'infra spam' was so dominant pre-1.11 that Paradox halved infra levels from 10 to 5 and re-scoped it toward supply. No maintenance or operating costs: buildings are buy-once assets, so the economy only ever grows.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the single-queue legibility but AVOID the self-compounding single currency. Split construction inputs: capital (fungible, national) plus regional labor and materials (steel/cement) that are NOT freely teleportable across 4,600 provinces. In a 40-year Cold War game, buildings must have operating costs (power, labor, maintenance) so growth is a portfolio choice, not compound interest — this is also exactly where planned vs market economies should diverge: the planned economy gets a literal state construction queue (Gosplan), the market economy gets investment flows it can only steer with fiscal/monetary levers, not directly assign.

systems.how_it_works: Two factory types: civilian (build/trade/consumer goods) and military (equipment). Mil factories output base ~4.5 units/day per line, modified by Factory Output bonuses. Each production line has Production Efficiency growing from a base 10% toward a researchable cap (50% base, up to 80-100% with tech), quadratically over months; switching equipment types resets or slashes efficiency, mitigated by 'efficiency retention' tech and the Dispersed vs Concentrated Industry mutually-exclusive research branch (Concentrated: +75% output; Dispersed: faster retooling/retention and bomb resistance). Efficiency is tracked per-factory, so veteran lines are precious.
systems.strengths: Production efficiency is HoI4's best economic idea: it makes retooling genuinely costly, rewards commitment and planning ahead, and creates the authentic dilemma of 'keep making obsolete equipment at 90% efficiency or retool to the new model at 10%'. Concentrated vs Dispersed is a real strategic identity choice (efficiency vs resilience).
systems.weaknesses: Civ/mil is a binary, and conversion (civ→mil at reduced cost) is a micro trick rather than a modeled war-mobilization process. Consumer goods are a pure dead-weight tax with zero gameplay — the civilian population consumes nothing specific and living standards don't exist. Nothing depreciates; a 1936 factory is identical in 1948. Late-game you have hundreds of factories and the interesting scarcity evaporates.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT production-efficiency/retooling friction wholesale — it is even more thematically correct for the Cold War (retooling from T-54 to T-62, B-47 to B-52 lines; the MiG design-bureau lock-in). But REPLACE the consumer-goods tax with a real civilian sector: consumer goods should be an output households actually demand, satisfying it should drive legitimacy/stability, and the planned economy's chronic consumer-goods shortage vs the market's consumer abundance should be a core, visible asymmetry — that IS the systems competition. Add capital depreciation so both blocs must run to stand still, which naturally models Soviet 1970s stagnation without scripting it.

systems.how_it_works: Base HoI4 has NO electricity system at all — power is implicit in factories. Only in Götterdämmerung (2024) did civil nuclear appear: the Nuclear Reactor special project unlocks reactor buildings, and a later 'Commercial Nuclear Reactor' project gives a building granting state-wide industry bonuses; reactors also passively add +0.01%/day nuclear breakthrough progress each, coupling civil power to the weapons program.
systems.strengths: The Götterdämmerung coupling of civilian reactors to weapons-program progress is a genuinely good idea: civil nuclear as both an economic asset and a proliferation pathway.
systems.weaknesses: Eight years without any power grid meant coal, hydro, and electrification — central facts of 1930s-50s industrialization (TVA, Dnieper dam, GOELRO) — simply don't exist. The retrofit is a bonus-granting building, not a grid: no generation/consumption balance, no brownouts, no coal dependency.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT a real but coarse power layer: provinces/regions have generation (coal/hydro/oil, later nuclear) and industry+cities have demand; deficit throttles factory throughput regionally. This is the missing link HoI4 never had, and for a Cold War game it's load-bearing — electrification of the Third World is an influence-warfare instrument (Aswan Dam!), civil reactors are dual-use proliferation on-ramps (Atoms for Peace), and power-plant construction is a natural showcase project for planned economies. Keep it aggregate (regional grids, not per-province wires) to survive 4,600 provinces.

systems.how_it_works: Each state has a fixed population; conscription law sets the recruitable fraction: Disarmed 1%, Volunteer Only 1.5%, Limited 2.5%, Extensive 5%, Service by Requirement 10%, All Adults 20%, Scraping the Barrel 25%, with escalating debuffs (e.g. -10% factory output and -40% construction speed at the top laws — the only place HoI4 models the labor/soldier tradeoff). Population grows a token ~1.5%/year. Non-core states yield only 2% of their manpower (98% penalty). Manpower is a single undifferentiated pool: no age structure, no skill, no urbanization, and factories require zero workers.
systems.strengths: Simple and readable; the conscription-law debuffs at least gesture at guns-vs-labor. The non-core penalty crudely prevents conquered-population snowballing.
systems.weaknesses: Population does nothing except fill divisions. In a game with real census data this is the biggest waste imaginable: no demographic transition, no rural→urban migration, no education/skill, no baby boom, no labor as a production input. The 98% non-core penalty is a hack in place of modeling loyalty. Community has complained for years that manpower is a bucket, not a society.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is OUR biggest differentiation opportunity given real 1950 per-province population. ADOPT labor as an actual factor of production: provinces have workforces split rural/urban; industrialization pulls labor off farms (which must not crater food output — see agriculture); education investment converts raw labor to skilled labor gating high-tech industry. Model the demographic transition (high growth in the decolonizing world, slowing growth in the developed world) — it drives the entire strategic arc 1950-1991 and makes the Third World the demographic prize both blocs court. Conscription then competes with the economy for the SAME workers, which HoI4 only fakes with flat debuffs.

systems.how_it_works: Does not exist in HoI4. There is no food resource, no farms, no rationing; blockades and strategic bombing affect war support and resources but nobody starves. Older Paradox titles (HoI3, Victoria) and mods (Kaiserreich, TNO, Black ICE) add food/consumer layers precisely because of this gap.
systems.strengths: Its absence keeps HoI4 focused and avoids famine-management tedium — a defensible cut for a 5-year wargame.
systems.weaknesses: Indefensible for a Cold War economic-competition game: collectivization famines, the Virgin Lands campaign, Soviet grain imports from the USA (the 1972 'Great Grain Robbery'), the Green Revolution, and food aid as influence currency are all pillars of the era. A planned-vs-market comparison without agriculture omits the planned economy's most famous failure mode.
systems.lesson_for_1950: BUILD what HoI4 skipped, but coarse: per-region agricultural output (land × labor × mechanization/fertilizer tech), national food balance, surplus exportable as trade/influence, deficit forcing imports, rationing (stability hit), or famine. The killer feature: collectivization as a planned-economy policy choice that frees labor and boosts state extraction while risking output collapse — letting the USSR player authentically face Khrushchev's dilemma, and making US grain sales to the USSR a détente-era lever. Keep it at the national/regional balance-sheet level, never per-province micromanagement.

systems.how_it_works: Six strategic resources (oil, steel, aluminum, rubber, tungsten, chromium) exist as per-state flow rates (not stockpiles, except oil→fuel). Production lines demand units; each missing unit imposes up to -5% output on the line. Local infrastructure raises state resource extraction. Trade: any country buys 8 resource units per civilian factory sent to the seller; price is fixed and identical regardless of scarcity, distance, or relations; trade law (Free Trade→Closed Economy) sets how much of your resources are forcibly exported vs kept, with Free Trade paradoxically giving the best research/output bonuses. Convoys carry trade and can be raided.
systems.strengths: Civ-factories-as-currency is elegant and self-balancing: buying resources visibly costs you construction capacity, and exporters gain usable industrial capacity. Resource shortages degrading (not stopping) production is good design. Trade routes being interdictable ties economy to the war map.
systems.weaknesses: The community's verdict (long forum threads) is that it killed economic play: no prices, no scarcity, no hoarding, no market — resources are 'always available at the same price regardless of world supply/demand,' so befriending Sweden for iron ore is pointless. Fixed 8-per-factory means the market can't tighten. Resource extraction buildings are usually worse than just building civs and buying. No money exists at all.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the fixed-price barter market; the Cold War needs actual prices. ADOPT a world market with floating prices for the market bloc (scarcity raises price → windfalls for producers → the 1973 oil shock emerges naturally) while the socialist bloc trades through negotiated bilateral deals and Comecon transfers at political prices — the two blocs literally using different trade rule sets is our economic-competition pillar made mechanical. Keep HoI4's 'shortage degrades output' curve and interdictable routes. Resource wealth in the Third World (Persian Gulf oil, Congolese uranium, Chilean copper) should be a primary driver of influence warfare.

systems.how_it_works: OLD system (pre-2024): research Atomic Research→Nuclear Reactor (~500 days each, late-tree), build reactor buildings (very expensive), then nukes accumulate passively — rate scaling with reactor count/level (roughly one bomb per reactor-year). Dropping one needs 75%+ air superiority; effect: damages buildings/units in one province, -war support. Universally criticized as an afterthought — a progress bar that majors AFK-complete by 1945-46, with trivial strategic effect. NEW system (Götterdämmerung special projects): build a Nuclear Research Facility, staff it with a scientist (skill/traits), accumulate 'breakthrough' points (+0.12%/day per research slot, +0.05%×skill from scientists, +0.01%/day per reactor), then run the project chain — Nuclear Reactor (90-day prototyping iterations of 10-15% random progress, costs steel/tungsten/chromium) → Fission Bomb → Thermonuclear Bomb (slower 5-10% iterations) → Nuclear Warheads (with MRBM tech, unlocks nuclear MRBM/ICBM). Facilities consume resources + supply daily; a raided/damaged facility or injured scientist halts progress; capturing enemy facilities grants +10% progress.
systems.strengths: The special-projects rework is exactly right in shape: a physical, geographic program (facilities you site, staff, supply) rather than a research bar. Prototyping with stochastic progress gives authentic program uncertainty. Scientists as named assets and facility capture/sabotage hooks directly into espionage — Manhattan Project spies became mechanically possible. Civil reactors feeding weapons breakthrough models dual-use.
systems.weaknesses: In base-game timeframe nukes still barely matter strategically once built (a province-damage button); AI handles them poorly. Randomness of prototype rolls can frustrate. The old system should be studied only as a cautionary tale: passive accumulation with no program visibility, no delivery-system distinction, no doctrine.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the Götterdämmerung shape and extend it — this is our core pillar, not a side system. Physical program: uranium sourcing (real geography — Congo, Czechoslovakia, Colorado), enrichment/reactor sites on the map, named scientists stealable by espionage, milestone tests that are public political events (detectable, deniable-ish, prestige and panic effects). Then go where HoI4 can't: separate warhead stockpile from delivery (bombers→MRBM→ICBM→SLBM), yield generations, and make the arsenal's meaning flow through the brinkmanship system (credibility, first-strike calculus, arms-control treaties as caps) rather than a 'delete province' button. Stochastic prototype progress is good — keep uncertainty, but let money/talent compress the variance.

systems.how_it_works: Since 1.6 (Man the Guns), oil converts to a stockpiled FUEL currency: each oil unit refines to 48 fuel/day (boosted to ~168 by refining tech); every country gets a small free base gain; synthetic refineries yield fuel directly without oil; fuel is stored up to a capacity from states + silo buildings, and consumed by tanks, planes, ships in operation — shortages slash speed/attack/mission effectiveness rather than immobilizing outright. Economy laws below War Economy cut fuel gain.
systems.strengths: One of HoI4's most successful retrofits: converting a flow resource into a stockpile with capacity made oil an actual war-planning object — Germany hoarding fuel for Barbarossa, Japan's oil clock after embargo both emerge naturally. Graceful degradation (penalties, not paralysis) is the right failure mode. Synthetics as an expensive strategic hedge is historically resonant.
systems.weaknesses: Only militaries consume fuel — the civilian economy runs on nothing, so an oil embargo can't hurt industry, which guts oil as a peacetime coercion tool. Fuel is invisible until war, so in long peace it's dead weight.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT stockpile-with-capacity and graceful degradation, but EXTEND consumption to the civilian economy and power grid: cars, industry, and electricity should burn oil so that embargoes, OPEC-style shocks, and the Soviet oil-export dependency work in peacetime — in a Cold War game oil coercion IS the gameplay (Suez 1956, 1973 embargo, Reagan-era price war bleeding Soviet hard currency). Market economies should feel shocks through price; planned economies through physical allocation and queues — same shock, different rule set.

systems.how_it_works: The 'planned economy' in HoI4 is a ladder of economy laws: Civilian Economy (35% consumer goods, -30% factory construction speed) → Early/Partial/War Economy (20%, +buffs) → Total Mobilization (10% consumer goods, -3% recruitable manpower), gated by war support/tension and costing 150 political power to shift. Plus trade law, and scripted national devices (MEFO bills, Soviet five-year-plan focuses, US depression spirits). All countries, fascist or liberal, use the same law ladder — ideology changes numbers, never rules.
systems.strengths: Laws-as-mobilization-dial is readable and creates a real timing game (getting War Economy early is a huge edge). Political-power gating means economic transformation competes with other political actions. MEFO bills show scripted debt-with-a-timebomb can work.
systems.weaknesses: This is precisely what our game must NOT copy: planned vs market is a stat-modifier reskin, not different systems. There is no money, no budget, no inflation, no investment choice for market economies, no plan targets for command economies. 'Total Mobilization' is just better numbers, not a strained society. Everything economic is one ladder plus focus-tree candy.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the universal law ladder; build two genuinely different rule sets. Command economy: the player IS the planner — sets five-year-plan output targets by sector, directly allocates labor/materials/capital, gets certainty and mobilization speed, but suffers systemic costs (plan-fulfillment gaming, quality malus, innovation drag, shortage queues feeding unrest) that worsen with economic complexity over decades. Market economy: the player does NOT directly own factories — steers via budget, taxes, interest rates, subsidies, and procurement contracts; private investment chases profitability (sometimes not where you want it), but delivers compounding productivity and consumer legitimacy. Mobilization for the market player is politically expensive and slow (Korea War rearmament), trivially fast for the planner. If a player can't articulate why the two blocs FEEL different to play in the first hour, we've failed the pillar.

key_takeaways: Kill the compound-interest opening: HoI4's civ-snowball exists because one fungible asset both builds everything and builds itself, with no operating costs. Give every building upkeep (labor, power, maintenance) and split construction inputs (capital + regional labor + materials), and the 'solved' build order dies without any artificial caps.

Production efficiency/retooling friction is HoI4's single best-loved economic mechanic — adopt it and generalize it: committed capacity that is costly to repurpose is the perfect engine for arms-race dynamics, military-industrial-complex lock-in, and the planner's dilemma of quantity-today vs quality-tomorrow.

The Götterdämmerung special-projects rework proves weapons programs should be physical and geographic (sited facilities, named scientists, resource inputs, stochastic prototypes, sabotage/capture hooks) — build our nuclear program in that shape from day one, then differentiate warheads from delivery systems and route all strategic meaning through brinkmanship rather than a damage button.

HoI4's fixed-price barter trade (8 resources per civ factory, no scarcity, no money) is its most-criticized economic choice; a Cold War game needs floating world-market prices for the capitalist bloc and negotiated bilateral/Comecon deals for the socialist bloc — asymmetric trade RULES, not asymmetric modifiers, are how 'economic systems competition' becomes mechanical.

HoI4 treats population as an ammo bucket and has no food, no power grid, and no civilian consumption — the four systems it lacks (labor as production input, agriculture, electricity, household consumption/living standards) are exactly the four arenas where planned and market economies historically diverged, and with real 1950 province populations they are our clearest differentiation from HoI4.

Extend every scarcity system into peacetime: fuel/oil, food, and consumer goods must matter when no one is shooting, because a 1950-1991 game is 90% peace — embargoes, grain deals, and oil shocks need civilian demand to bite, and HoI4's war-only consumption model is why its long peaces feel dead.

reports.games: Victoria 3 (Paradox, 2022; mechanics as of patches ~1.0–1.9, incl. 1.2 economic-law rework and 1.5 construction rebalance). Sources: vic3.paradoxwikis.com (Market, Construction, Building, Pops, Standard of living, Investment pool, Electricity pages), Paradox dev diaries #13 (Standard of Living) and #72 (Economic Law Changes), Paradox forum design critiques ("Far too many words on Victoria 3's Gameplay Loop", "The Fundamentally Broken Economics of Victoria 3"), Steam community guides/discussions (electricity handbook, construction threads), pcgamesn/thegamer/games.gg guides.
key_takeaways: Construction-as-universal-throughput is V3's best and worst idea at once. One fungible 'construction points' resource that everything competes for is legible and creates real opportunity cost — but because construction sectors themselves are buildings, 'build more builders' is always the dominant move and the whole game collapses into a GDP-snowball idle loop. If we adopt a throughput resource, its supply must NOT be purchasable with itself: gate ours on separate constraints (skilled labor, cement/steel physical output, energy) so the bottleneck migrates over the campaign instead of being solved once.

V3's price formula (base price x [1 +/- 0.75 x order imbalance], hard-capped at 25%-175%) is computationally cheap — attractive at our 4,600-province scale — but it is a ratio, not a clearing mechanism: surpluses vanish, shortages conjure goods, and money is literally created/destroyed by mismatches. For a Cold War game where grain reserves, strategic stockpiles, and queues-outside-empty-shops are THE theme, we must add inventories: unsold goods persist as stockpiles that depress future prices (market side) or fill state reserves (planned side). Stockpiles are not a nice-to-have for us; they are the mechanical substrate of brinkmanship (oil embargoes, grain deals, blockades).

V3's command economy is a confession of failure we should study: it just seizes the investment pool as lump-sum cash and otherwise runs the same price economy with different sliders. That is exactly the trap to avoid. Our planned economies should not see prices as the primary signal at all — they should allocate physical inputs against output quotas (with plan-fulfillment lying, hoarding by enterprises, and shortage propagation as the failure modes), while market economies get V3's genuinely good idea: an autonomous private investment queue the player can only tax, subsidize, and regulate, never directly command.

Standard-of-living-driven demographics are V3's quietest triumph: birth and mortality both fall with SoL but mortality falls faster, so the demographic transition, urbanization, and starvation crises all emerge from one curve (mortality spikes below SoL 5, growth peaks ~SoL 15, floors of 0.6% birth / 0.45% mortality above SoL 25) with zero player micromanagement. With real 1950 population data per province, adopt this almost verbatim — it lets the player watch the actual postwar baby boom, Third World population explosion, and Eastern Bloc stagnation emerge, and gives famine (Great Leap Forward-style) as a consequence of planning failure rather than a scripted event.

Subsistence agriculture as the default occupant of arable land is the single best mechanic to steal for modeling the 1950 Third World: peasants on subsistence plots are a visible, province-level reservoir of latent labor and latent political grievance, and every development strategy — Soviet-style collectivization, land reform, cash-crop export dependency — is a different answer to 'how do we get these people off subsistence farms, and who eats the transition cost?' V3 never made that choice ideological; for a Cold War game it IS the ideological competition, so make each bloc's answer a different rule set with different failure modes (procurement crises vs. commodity price dependency).

Electricity as a non-tradeable local input good that gates advanced production methods is great tech-era pacing but became 'micromanagement hell' at V3's ~100-state granularity — at 4,600 provinces it would be unplayable. Model power as regional grids (a network layer over provinces) rather than per-province goods, and make nuclear power the deliberate bridge V3 never had: civilian reactors as a prestige good and plutonium path that couples the electricity system to the weapons program, so 'Atoms for Peace' vs. weapons-grade enrichment is a real allocation decision inside one system.

systems.how_it_works: All building in V3 flows through one abstract resource: construction points, added weekly to a queue. Base +10/week per country; everything else comes from Construction Sector buildings, whose output per level depends on production method: wooden buildings ~10 points consuming wood+fabric, iron-frame ~30 consuming iron/tools, steel-frame ~90, arc-welded ~150 (guide figures: up to 60/150/450 per fully-upgraded building tier), each tier consuming progressively more expensive inputs (steel, glass, explosives) and employing fewer laborers per point. Buildings cost 100-800 points (unique buildings 2,500; canals 5,000). A per-country 'max weekly progress' caps how many points one queue item can absorb; overflow spills to the next item, so wide queues matter. The queue is split into a government lane (paid from treasury) and a private lane (goods paid from the investment pool, wages always from treasury), with the split set by the Economic System law; an underused lane's points spill to the other. Construction efficiency modifiers (local sectors, decrees +10%, bureaucracy surplus up to +10%) multiply progress per point, floored at 5%.
systems.strengths: Brilliantly legible: one number tells you your nation's total capacity to change itself, and every build decision is a visible opportunity cost against everything else. The input-goods coupling is the best part — construction demand for wood/iron/steel is the early economy's largest customer, so industrializing your construction industry literally industrializes the country, and construction cost falls as you make its inputs cheap. The tiered production methods create a satisfying 'retool the builders' cadence each tech era.
systems.weaknesses: The defining degenerate strategy of the game: construction sectors are themselves buildings, so points buy more points. Optimal play is to pour 30-50%+ of the economy into construction sectors and snowball; the Paradox forum critique 'Far too many words on Victoria 3's Gameplay Loop' argues every other subsystem exists to feed this resource-deficit-construction loop, and players describe late-game V3 as 'an idle game with extra strings.' Because construction only needs ~4 goods for most of the game, industrial strategy narrows to feeding the builder. Patch 1.5 raised costs and made sectors consume goods proportional to activity, softening but not solving it. Also ahistorical: nations cannot surge construction in crisis (war rebuilding) without having pre-built the sector.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT, with the feedback loop cut. A national 'construction capacity' resource is right for a 1950 game (Five-Year Plans and the Interstate Highway System are both stories about allocating scarce construction). But supply of capacity must come from things capacity cannot directly buy: cement/steel/machine-tool physical output, skilled-labor pools, and energy, each a separate constraint that binds at different eras. Keep V3's two-lane queue (state lane vs. private lane) — it is the cleanest possible expression of our planned-vs-market pillar: a command economy is 100% state lane with quota targets; a market economy's private lane builds autonomously from profit signals and the player only shapes it with taxes, subsidies, and regulation. Add crisis surge (war economy laws temporarily convert civilian industry to construction at an efficiency penalty) so capacity is not purely pre-committed.

systems.how_it_works: The building is the economic atom: every farm, mine, factory, port, and government office is a building in a state, expanded in discrete levels. Each level employs a fixed slate of pops by profession (laborers, machinists, engineers, clerks, capitalists...) set by its production methods, buys inputs and sells outputs at local prices, pays wages that float with labor-market competition, accumulates a cash reserve, and pays dividends to owner pops when reserves are full. Owner pops route a share of dividends into the national investment pool: farmers/machinists 10%, bureaucrats/engineers 15%, shopkeepers/clergy 20%, aristocrats 20-25%, capitalists 30% (+25pp for aristocrats under Industry Banned). The pool funds the private construction queue; under laissez-faire, private investors build manufacturing plus select raw industries (wood, fishing, oil, infrastructure); under command economy the pool is simply confiscated as treasury income and contributions stop. Post-1.7, ownership itself is modeled (buildings owned by manor houses, financial districts, or foreign countries), letting capital and dividends flow across borders.
systems.strengths: Buildings-as-atom is widely praised as the most legible economy Paradox has shipped: you can always answer 'why is this unprofitable' by opening the building and reading its input prices and wages. Employment creates a real labor market — expanding industry pulls pops out of subsistence farming, raises wages, and shifts political power, so industrialization is a social transformation, not a production multiplier. The investment pool elegantly makes private capital a distinct actor with its own preferences.
systems.weaknesses: Auto-expansion + modifier stacking degenerates: over-profitable buildings expand forever, crashing their own output prices, because profitability rather than expected marginal return drives AI investment. Players long complained of millions idling in the pool ('no potential private constructions to invest in') — private investment AI is only as good as its build-target heuristics. Wages and employment per level are uniform enough that the 'firm' has no interior life: no productivity differences, no management, no obsolete capital stock — a 1890 level and a 1930 level of the same building are identical except for the production method toggle. Command economy is mechanically hollow: same buildings, same prices, pool seized, done.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT buildings/enterprises-as-atom and the ownership layer — for us, ownership IS the Cold War (nationalization of Suez, United Fruit, Iranian oil are core gameplay). But give enterprises vintage: capital built in 1950 should embody 1950 productivity and require modernization investment, so the USSR's 1970s stagnation (old capital, no exit mechanism) emerges naturally — planned economies get no bankruptcy, so obsolete plants persist and drag productivity; market economies destroy and replace. Make the investment pool a genuine market-economy-only actor with return-seeking heuristics the player influences but never commands, and give planned economies a wholly different expansion driver: plan targets that allocate construction and inputs by quota, with over-fulfillment rewards distorting reported data.

systems.how_it_works: Electricity (base price 30) is a late-game good produced by Power Plant buildings — production methods burn coal or oil, or use hydro (no fuel, geography-gated) — and it is strictly local: produced and consumed within one state, never traded or transported. Advanced production methods across the economy (textile mills, steel mills, shipyards, railways, automation PMs) require electricity as an input and yield throughput/labor-saving bonuses; pops also consume it for household needs once available. Later patches added high-voltage electricity variants and state traits boosting output. Because throughput bonuses scale with concentration, splitting plants across many states loses efficiency — but demand exists in every industrial state, forcing plant-per-state micromanagement. V3's timeframe (1836-1936) means no nuclear power exists.
systems.strengths: Excellent era-gating: electrification is a palpable second industrial revolution — a whole economy's production methods flip when power arrives, and hydro geography (Norway, Alpine states) creates real regional character. Making it non-tradeable correctly captures that pre-grid power was local and forces industrial geography decisions instead of one national pool.
systems.weaknesses: The Paradox forum thread title says it: 'Electricity is micromanagement hell.' Per-state balancing of an untradeable good across dozens of states, with throughput bonuses punishing exactly the distribution the mechanic demands, is pure tedium. No transmission/grid layer ever arrives even by 1936, which is ahistorical. Shortages silently throttle every downstream building via the generic shortage penalty, making diagnosis annoying.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT into regional grids. At 4,600 provinces, per-province power is unplayable; model named grid networks (TVA, RAO UES precursors, national grids) as a layer above provinces — plants feed a grid, provinces draw from it, interconnection is buildable, and blackouts/brownouts throttle industry grid-wide. This preserves V3's good idea (power as a physical input gating modern industry, with geography mattering via hydro and coal basins) while killing the tedium. Then do what V3's timeframe forbade: make civilian nuclear power a first-class bridge to the weapons pillar — reactors produce electricity AND plutonium, enrichment capacity serves either fuel or bombs, so every kilowatt-vs-kiloton allocation is a real decision, and 'Atoms for Peace' reactor exports become an influence-warfare tool that seeds proliferation risk.

systems.how_it_works: Pops (grouped by profession, culture, religion, workplace) grow via birth rate minus mortality, both functions primarily of Standard of Living, a 1-99 scale derived from what wealth of goods a pop can afford. Below SoL 5, mortality spikes (starvation); from SoL 5-15 mortality falls quickly while birth rate falls slowly, so growth peaks around SoL 15; above ~25, floors apply (0.60% birth, 0.45% mortality) and growth flattens near +0.15%/yr. Modifiers: Rights of Women laws, Health System institution, pollution, devastation, working conditions. Pops whose SoL falls below their expected SoL (rising with literacy/skill) radicalize; SoL gains create loyalists. Employment, wages, and consumption feed SoL, closing the loop with the building economy.
systems.strengths: One elegant curve produces the entire demographic transition, urbanization, mass migration, and political radicalization as emergent phenomena — widely considered the beating heart of the game. It gives economic growth a purpose beyond GDP: the map's people visibly get richer or starve, and 'line goes up' has a human referent. Radicalism-from-immiseration means recessions have political teeth.
systems.weaknesses: Mostly hands-off, which is fine, but the SoL basket is opaque (players struggle to see WHY SoL moved), and because mortality responds instantly to prices, brief market glitches can cause absurd death spikes. Migration heuristics are erratic. Homogeneous pop groups hide distributional questions — no within-profession inequality.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT nearly wholesale — this is the best-fit V3 system for our game and our real 1950 province-level population data is the perfect substrate. Calibrate the SoL-growth curve to reproduce the historical 1950-1990 trajectories (baby boom, Third World explosion, demographic transition timing) as the no-intervention baseline, then let policy bend it. Two Cold War-specific additions: (1) make consumption-goods SoL a legitimacy resource that planned economies chronically underprovide — the guns-vs-butter squeeze that actually eroded the Eastern Bloc — so a player running a command economy feels the kitchen-debate pressure; (2) tie emigration pressure to SoL gaps across the Iron Curtain, making border regimes (Berlin Wall) a real policy response to a real mechanic, not an event.

systems.how_it_works: Each state has fixed arable land. All arable land not occupied by built agriculture is automatically covered by Subsistence Farms employing peasants, who produce a trickle of food/fabric mostly self-consumed, earn near-nothing, pay almost no tax, and cannot promote into skilled professions. Built farms/ranches/plantations (rye, wheat, rice, livestock, coffee, cotton, opium, etc.) occupy that land, employ fewer workers per acre at higher productivity, and sell into the market. Building them both displaces subsistence land directly and crashes staple prices, cutting peasant income and pushing peasants toward wage work — but can create transitional unemployment since one farm level employs fewer people than the subsistence plots it replaces. Food price feeds pop SoL; grain shortage means SoL collapse means starvation mortality below SoL 5.
systems.strengths: The single most praised structural idea in V3: pre-industrial society is the default state of the map, not an absence. Development means pulling people OUT of subsistence, and the mechanic makes visible the classic development economics tradeoff — productivity vs. employment, cash crops vs. food security. Famine emerges from prices and war devastation rather than scripts.
systems.weaknesses: The transition is frictionless and apolitical: no landlords resisting land reform, no procurement problem, no collectivization option — historically the central agrarian questions of the era. Cash-crop monoculture carries no risk (no world-price shocks, no soil exhaustion). Because food is just another market good with capped prices, true famine dynamics (hoarding, entitlement failure) can't occur; the ±75% price cap means bread can never become unaffordable enough.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT subsistence-as-default-land-use — in 1950, most of humanity is peasants and this mechanic is exactly how to represent China, India, and the decolonizing world at province granularity. Then ADD what V3 omits, because it is our game's ideological core: three rival exits from subsistence as distinct rule sets — collectivization (fast state grain procurement, high short-term famine risk, peasant resistance; enables rapid forced industrialization à la USSR/PRC), market land reform (slow, raises rural SoL and food output, creates smallholder conservative politics à la Japan/Taiwan/South Korea), and plantation export dependency (immediate foreign exchange, world-price shock exposure, foreign ownership as an influence-warfare lever). Uncap food prices past shortage thresholds and let procurement quotas fail — the Great Leap famine must be a possible outcome of player choices, not an event.

systems.how_it_works: Raw resources are buildings on state-limited deposits: mines (coal, iron, sulfur, lead, gold), oil rigs, rubber plantations, logging camps, fisheries — each state has fixed discovered potential, with some deposits hidden behind prospecting techs (notably oil and rubber, which explode in importance late-game). Output responds to price like any building; there is no depletion. Goods are 43-odd types flowing through the market system: local price = MAPI x market price + (1-MAPI) x state price, base MAPI 75%; market access depends on infrastructure and convoys. Shortage (buy orders ≥ 2x sell orders) throttles consumer-building throughput -5% then -1%/day to -50% (-75% if supply totally absent). Trade routes to other markets move goods via trade centers with capacity limits.
systems.strengths: Deposit geography creates genuine strategic geography — the scramble for rubber and oil emerges from the tech tree flipping demand curves, which is exactly the right way to make imperialism economically motivated rather than scripted. The shortage-throughput mechanic makes supply chains fail gracefully and visibly rather than binarily.
systems.weaknesses: No depletion and no stockpiles: you cannot hoard strategic materials, embargo effects are instantaneous price shifts rather than reserve drawdowns, and wartime blockade bites in days not months. The 2:1 shortage threshold plus price caps means economies are far too tolerant of scarcity. Trade is famously weak/AI-driven — players call trade route micromanagement the worst UI in the game, and arbitrage exploits between markets persist.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT with stockpiles as first-class objects. For a Cold War game, strategic reserves are gameplay: the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve concept, Soviet grain purchases of 1972, COCOM embargoes, chrome/titanium chokepoints. Every strategic good (oil, grain, uranium, rare metals) needs national reserve levels that buffer embargoes and are themselves intelligence targets and brinkmanship instruments — 'how many months of oil does Japan-analog have' should be a question with a number. Keep deposit geography and prospecting (Persian Gulf oil discoveries, uranium in the Congo/Kazakhstan are 1950s plot engines), add slow depletion for oil only, and make East-West trade flow through explicit politically-gated channels rather than V3's ambient world market — trade permission IS the influence-warfare weapon.

systems.how_it_works: V3 (1836-1936) has no nuclear weapons; its nearest analogs are megaprojects — unique buildings (2,500 construction) and canals (5,000, ~5-10x a normal building) that monopolize construction throughput for years — and the tech-innovation system (capped weekly innovation points from universities, spread across research). There is no secrecy, no discrete milestone progress, and no dual-use resource coupling anywhere in the design.
systems.strengths: The megaproject pattern is instructive: forcing a giant project through the same universal throughput queue as ordinary industry makes its opportunity cost brutally tangible — Suez means years of not building steel mills, a genuinely felt sacrifice rather than a separate 'wonder' currency.
systems.weaknesses: Not applicable as a weapons model — but note V3's research system weakness: innovation is a smooth undifferentiated stream, so nothing feels like a program with milestones, gates, and failure risk. That is precisely the wrong texture for a Manhattan/Sputnik-era game.
systems.lesson_for_1950: Take only the opportunity-cost lesson: a nuclear weapons program should draw from the SAME scarce national pools as civilian economy — construction throughput, scientists, electricity (enrichment consumed ~10% of US electricity in the early 1950s; Oak Ridge is an electricity story), and fissile-material production shared with civilian reactors — so the bomb is a rival claim on the economy, not a parallel minigame. Structure it as discrete gated milestones (reactor criticality, enrichment cascade, implosion test) with uncertainty, visible to rivals through the espionage pillar via observable inputs (calutron electricity draw, uranium ore purchases — historically how intelligence actually tracked programs). V3 proves the anti-pattern to avoid: smooth accumulating points with no texture.

systems.how_it_works: V3's economic systems are laws modifying one shared engine. Prices everywhere follow price = base x [1 + 0.75 x clamp((buy-sell)/min(buy,sell), ±1)], capped at 25%-175% of base; mismatched orders create or destroy money outright (buyers can pay for 100 units while sellers are paid for 120 — the ~£340 difference materializes from nothing). Laws then vary: Laissez-Faire (big investment pool contributions, private queue builds most industry, government construction share small), Interventionism (balanced split, government can build anything), Agrarianism (pool favors agriculture, aristocrat-driven), Cooperative Ownership (workers own buildings, pool from worker dividends), Command Economy (investment pool confiscated as lump-sum treasury income, all contributions stop, ~100% government construction queue, government owns buildings). Dev diary #72 (patch 1.2) explicitly acknowledged post-release ambition to make systems 'mechanically deeper' than modifier swaps.
systems.strengths: The law-based framing means economic systems are political outcomes — you must win an internal power struggle to change systems, which correctly makes economics downstream of politics. The two-queue construction split is a genuinely good minimal model of the public/private capital allocation difference. The price formula, whatever its sins, is O(goods x markets) cheap and always produces a legible number.
systems.weaknesses: This is the heart of the 'fake prices' critique (forum thread 'The Fundamentally Broken Economics of Victoria 3'): prices are an instantaneous ratio, not a clearing mechanism — no inventories, surpluses sold 'to the void,' shortages filled ex nihilo, money created/destroyed by imbalance, the ±75% cap preventing real scarcity pricing, and local-vs-market price differences vanishing into thin air. Worse for our purposes: command economy is the SAME price economy with the pool confiscated — planning has no plan, no quotas, no allocation problem, no soft budget constraints. The most interesting economic question of V3's own era-successor is answered with a modifier.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the shared-engine-plus-modifiers approach; this is the pillar our game exists to do right. Market economies: keep V3-style emergent prices but with inventories so markets actually clear over time (surplus accumulates as stock, depressing price gradually; scarcity can exceed any cap), and autonomous profit-seeking investment. Planned economies: run on a genuinely different rule set — the player (as Gosplan) sets output quotas and allocates physical inputs and construction among sectors via a material-balance interface; 'prices' are administered accounting numbers; the failure modes are the historical ones (hoarding by enterprises, plan-fulfillment misreporting that corrupts the player's OWN information display, shortage propagation down input chains, soft budget constraints keeping dead plants alive). Crucially, misreporting means the planned-economy player's dashboard shows plan data, not truth — espionage-pillar synergy: your own statistics are an intelligence problem. The two systems should feel like different games competing on output, exactly as the pillar demands; V3 demonstrates that anything less reads as one economy wearing two hats.

reports.games: Victoria 2 (Paradox, 2010) and Europa Universalis IV (Paradox, 2013). Vic2 is the emergent-simulation pole: all economic value flows from ~pops with needs, jobs, and politics; the player steers indirectly. EU4 is the abstraction pole: provinces carry three development numbers and buildings; the player buys outcomes directly with 'monarch point' mana. Sources consulted: vic2.paradoxwikis.com (Promotion, National focus & population guide, Industrialization guide), eu4.paradoxwikis.com (Buildings, Development), ACOUP 'Teaching Paradox: Victoria II' parts I-III (acoup.blog), PDM wiki economy pages, Paradox forum threads on monarch-point critique and manufactory ROI, Steam community threads on artisan/capitalist AI failure, gamedeveloper.com Vic3 economy deep-dive.

systems.how_it_works: Population is chunked into POPs: units of up to ~100k people with a type (12 types in 3 strata — poor: farmers, labourers, craftsmen, soldiers, slaves; middle: artisans, clerks, clergy, bureaucrats, officers; rich: aristocrats, capitalists), plus culture, religion, literacy, money, militancy, consciousness, and ideology/issue distributions. Each POP buys three tiers of needs from the world market out of its own income: life needs (food, basics — unmet life needs cause starvation and militancy), everyday needs, luxury needs; need baskets scale with strata and grow as inventions are discovered. Promotion/demotion is a two-roll system defined in POPtypes.txt: fulfillment of needs, literacy (each +10% literacy raises promotion, lowers demotion), and national focus determine whether e.g. farmers become craftsmen or craftsmen demote back. Growth is per-province: a base rate (~0.5%/yr scale) modified by the province's static Life Rating (provinces below a life-rating threshold barely grow; health techs raise effective life rating several % per tech) and by life-needs fulfillment. Migration is emergent: POPs move internally toward provinces with jobs and higher life rating; militancy, unemployment, and lack of political/social reforms push emigration, and countries' reform level + economy generates immigrant attraction (the New World vacuums up European emigrants). Assimilation to primary culture is slow and province-dependent.
systems.strengths: The single best-loved system in Paradox history. Because pops are the source of ALL value (tax, soldiers, factory labor, research via clergy/clerk ratios), every policy becomes a demographic question, and long-term strategy emerges: raise literacy now to industrialize in 30 years; pass reforms to attract immigrants; keep life needs cheap to grow population. Nothing is scripted — the great Irish/German emigration to the USA happens because the sim's push/pull factors fire. Players describe outcomes ('my craftsmen demoted because the factory closed because cotton got expensive because the ACW happened') as stories the system wrote.
systems.weaknesses: Opaque: the two-roll promotion logic, need multipliers, and migration weights are invisible in the UI; players learn them from wikis or not at all. Micromanagement ceiling: national focus juggling to promote craftsmen/clergy state-by-state is tedium, not strategy. Performance: late-game POP splitting (by culture x religion x type x province) explodes object counts. Life Rating is a static magic number that makes Siberia/Africa permanently unattractive regardless of player action. Population growth is too uniform — no demographic transition, so 1936 Europe grows like 1836 Europe.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT, aggressively coarsened. With ~4,600 provinces and real 1950 population, do NOT do 12-type per-province pops — do 3-5 cohorts (rural, urban worker, educated/professional, elite; plus per-province ethnicity where it matters politically) with needs and a loyalty/ideology axis, simulated at region level and only displayed per-province. Crucially, ADD what Vic2 lacked: the demographic transition. 1950-1991 is the era where birth rates diverge — model birth/death rates as functions of urbanization, healthcare investment, and female education, so the Third World population boom, the baby boom, and late-Soviet stagnation emerge and matter (manpower, food demand, unemployment-driven unrest). Replace static Life Rating with infrastructure/climate-derived habitability the player can invest in (Virgin Lands, irrigation). And make every pop-driven outcome inspectable: a 'why is this happening' panel is the difference between emergent depth and wiki homework.

systems.how_it_works: Factories exist at state (multi-province) level, one per good type, expandable in levels; each level employs up to 10,000 craftsmen plus clerks (optimal ~4:1 craftsmen:clerks; clerks boost output efficiency). Output = base × throughput (scales with employment % and input availability) × efficiency (clerk ratio, techs, bonuses). Factories buy input goods on the world market and pay wages from revenue; unprofitable factories run down cash reserves and close, firing their pops. Who builds depends on economic policy: under laissez-faire only capitalist POPs build/expand (an AI investor using their accumulated savings); under State Capitalism/Planned Economy the state builds with treasury money; interventionism allows subsidies. Artisans are a parallel system: a middle-strata POP type that individually buys inputs and hand-produces goods, competing with factories on the same market. Tech gives factories (not artisans) throughput/efficiency bonuses, so factories undercut artisans over the century.
systems.strengths: Industrialization is a genuine strategy with prerequisites, not a build queue: you need literate craftsmen (education), input access (trade/conquest), and demand. The factory-closes → craftsmen-demote → militancy-rises loop makes deindustrialization politically dangerous, which is historically true and mechanically elegant. Input-output chains (coal+iron→steel→machine parts) create real interdependence and make resource geography strategic.
systems.weaknesses: The capitalist AI is the most notorious failure in the game: capitalists build unprofitable factories, refuse to build profitable ones, and pile investment into whatever briefly shows margin. Skilled players learned the degenerate meta of cycling governments — install a planned/state-capitalist party to build a rational industrial base, then flip to laissez-faire for efficiency bonuses — gaming the policy system rather than engaging with it. Artisans are a death spiral: they persist unprofitably, suppress factory demand signals, then mass-bankrupt. Late-game global liquidity problems (money enters the world only via gold mines) cause economy-wide deflation no player action can fix. One-factory-type-per-state and per-state micromanagement of subsidies is tedious.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT — this is the closest existing template for our market-economy ruleset, and its failures are the spec for fixing it. Market economies in our game should have autonomous private investment (firms/capitalists respond to profitability), but three fixes are mandatory: (1) the investor AI's logic must be simple, published, and correct — 'invests in the highest-ROI sector meeting demand' — so the player can steer it with legible levers (interest rates, procurement contracts, tariffs, tax breaks) instead of fighting it; (2) never let a parallel legacy sector (Vic2's artisans) silently poison price signals — if we model informal/artisanal economies in the Third World, give them an explicit modernization mechanic; (3) policy switching must have transition costs (capital flight, strikes, lost institutional knowledge) so 'cycle the government' is never free. Keep input-output chains — steel/machine-tools/consumer-goods interdependence is the heart of Cold War economics — but at maybe 20-30 goods, not Vic2's ~50.

systems.domain: agriculture, food & resources (Vic2 RGOs and the world market)
systems.how_it_works: Every province has exactly one Resource Gathering Operation producing one fixed good (grain, cotton, coal, iron, oil...). Max workers = 40,000 × province size factor × (1 + terrain + RGO size modifiers); employed farmers (agricultural goods) or labourers (minerals) generate output = base production × throughput (employment %) × output efficiency (1 + aristocrat % in state — ~2% is optimal — + tech + terrain). RGOs cannot be built or switched; tech raises their output. All goods trade on a single global market with prices floating in bands around base price by supply/demand; crucially, countries buy in prestige order — great powers literally shop first, and low-prestige nations face empty shelves on scarce goods (machine parts famously). Food is not a survival system per se: grain/fish/cattle are life-needs goods, and unmet life needs slow growth and raise militancy rather than triggering explicit famine.
systems.strengths: Fixed resource geography makes the map strategically legible and makes conquest/sphere-of-influence economically motivated: you sphere Chile for the saltpeter, you want the Ruhr for coal. The single world market means distant events propagate — the US Civil War spikes world cotton prices and your textile industry feels it. Employment-based throughput ties resources back to population, so depopulated or illiterate regions genuinely underproduce.
systems.weaknesses: One-good-per-province is rigid: no crop choice, no discovering oil where there wasn't any (partially patched via events), no land-use tradeoff between food and cash crops. Prestige-ordered purchasing is an infamous absurdity — an economic queue determined by winning wars and sponsoring expeditions. No bilateral trade, no embargoes, no trade policy beyond tariff slider; you cannot blockade an economy in peacetime. Food security is invisible — no stockpiles, no famine as an event with political consequences, which for a game containing the Great Leap Forward era would be an unforgivable gap.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the resource geography, REPLACE the market. Fixed, map-based resource endowments (with discoverable oil/uranium deposits as explicit exploration mechanics) are correct for the Cold War — Persian Gulf oil, Katanga uranium/cobalt, Ukrainian grain should be why places matter. But Vic2's single prestige-ordered world market is precisely the wrong shape for 1950: build TWO overlapping trade systems as a core expression of the economic-competition pillar — a dollar-denominated market bloc (prices, currency reserves, embargo/CoCom export controls as policy) and a COMECON-style negotiated-barter bloc (bilateral quota agreements, subsidized oil-for-machinery deals), with the Third World as the contested zone choosing between them. Food must be explicit: per-country calorie balance from agriculture + imports, with stockpiles, and famine as a political catastrophe (legitimacy loss, unrest, international propaganda ammunition) — collectivization and the Green Revolution should both be playable gambles.

systems.how_it_works: The ruling party's economic policy sets who may build and fund industry: Laissez-Faire (only capitalists build factories/railroads; player cannot; factory subsidies forbidden; best output modifiers), Interventionism (capitalists build, player may subsidize and expand), State Capitalism (player builds with treasury, capitalists also may), Planned Economy (only the state builds; capitalists' investment role removed; worst efficiency modifiers). Combined with tariff and tax sliders (with strata-differentiated tax rates), this is the whole 'planning' toolkit. National Stockpile settings let the state buy military/construction goods from the market.
systems.strengths: This is, to date, the only mainstream grand-strategy attempt at making planned vs. market economies genuinely different RULE SETS rather than a modifier swap — under laissez-faire you literally lose the build button and must govern through incentives. When it works, it produces the real dilemma: state direction industrializes faster from a low base; markets allocate better at the frontier. That dilemma is historically true and is exactly our game's fourth pillar.
systems.weaknesses: The execution collapsed: because the capitalist AI was broken and efficiency modifiers were flat percentage bonuses, the 'market' side wasn't a different economic logic, just a worse UI over a dumb AI plus a stat bonus. Planned economy wasn't a planning system — no output targets, no plan fulfillment, no shortage economy, no soft budget constraints — just 'the player is the only builder.' Party-cycling exploit (noted above) let players harvest the best of both. Taxation/tariff sliders were the only fiscal instruments; no monetary policy at all.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the ambition, redesign the execution — this domain should be our game's crown jewel. Planned economy = an EU4-like direct-control layer with teeth: the player writes Five-Year Plans (allocate scarce material balances and skilled labor to sectors, set output targets), and the SIMULATION pushes back — plan fulfillment is gamed by managers (quantity over quality: the classic nail-factory problem as a mechanic), shortages cascade through input chains, prices carry no information so the player must find misallocation through reports (imperfect, lagged data as a design feature), and soft budget constraints mean failing enterprises never die without a political fight. Market economy = a Vic2-like indirect layer done right: autonomous firms with legible investment logic, steered via interest rates, defense procurement, tax policy, and trade — with business cycles the player must manage and stagflation as a possible failure state. The scoring question of the Cold War — growth rate vs. consumer welfare vs. military output — should be measurable in both systems so the ideological competition is a live scoreboard (kitchen debate as gameplay). Never let a country switch systems cheaply: transition = years of disruption (this is also your collapse-of-1989 endgame mechanic for free).

systems.domain: construction & development (EU4 development, monarch points, buildings)
systems.how_it_works: Each province has three development values (adm=tax, dip=production/trade, mil=manpower). The player spends monarch points — three mana pools generated monthly by ruler skill (0-6 per category) + advisors (+1..+5) — to raise dev: base cost ~50 points per click, inflated by the province's existing dev and terrain, deflated by modifiers (stacking -10/-20% ideas, prosperity, estates; forum meta identifies ~20-dev provinces as the efficiency sweet spot for institution-spawning). Buildings occupy limited slots (roughly 1 per 10 dev), cost ducats and 12 months: temple +40% local tax, workshop +50% local production, barracks +50% local manpower (each ~100 ducats), manufactory +1 good produced (~500 ducats). Manpower pool = mil dev × 250 × modifiers, regenerating over 10 years; buildings and dev, not people, are what war attrits (via devastation and sack).
systems.strengths: Ruthlessly legible: every choice is a clean, comparable transaction with visible ROI, decidable in five seconds. Development-as-terrain makes 'tall vs. wide' an actual choice, and building slots create a real composition decision (which two buildings does this province get?). Monarch points do successfully impose opportunity cost across domains — dev vs. tech vs. coring conquered land is a genuine strategic triage. It performs beautifully at scale, which matters for our 4,600 provinces.
systems.weaknesses: Monarch points are the most-criticized mechanic in Paradox's catalog: an arbitrary universal currency disconnected from any simulated reality (a genius king literally makes farmland more fertile), and because everything costs mana, everything becomes one flat optimization problem — the community consensus is that it began as elegant and bloated into 'mana pays for everything.' Dev-clicking has zero strategic content once the efficiency meta is known; it's a solved spreadsheet. Building ROI measured in decades while conquest pays instantly means the sim rewards ignoring the economy — 'EU4 is a snowballing game; field a bigger army instead' is the community's own verdict. No population means no demographic consequences of anything: you can lose every war and your provinces are back in 10 years.
systems.lesson_for_1950: SPLIT the lesson. AVOID mana absolutely: no abstract point pool generated by leader dice-rolls that buys unrelated outcomes. But ADOPT capacity currencies that the SIMULATION produces and that map to real 1950 bottlenecks: construction capacity (cement/steel/labor), administrative capacity (bureaucrats, literacy), and scarce specialists (engineers, nuclear physicists — the last doubling as the throttle on weapons programs). These give EU4's legibility ('I can build 3 things this year, which 3?') without its absurdity, because the player grows the currencies through the economy itself. Adopt building-slot-style scarcity per province/region so construction is about composition and location (put the steel mill near coal AND away from bomber range — Soviet Urals relocation logic as an actual decision). And take the ROI critique seriously in reverse: our game has no conquest snowball to outcompete investment, so construction CAN be the core loop — but only if payoffs land within a player-felt horizon (3-8 game-years) and are visible when they do.

systems.domain: population & growth (EU4 manpower abstraction, as contrast)
systems.how_it_works: EU4 has no population. 'Manpower' is a national pool (mil dev × 250 × modifiers, ~10-year full regen) drained by recruitment and combat reinforcement; 'sailors' mirrors it for navies. Provinces contribute tax/production/manpower as pure numbers; culture and religion are province labels affecting unrest and cost modifiers, not living groups. War exhaustion and devastation are temporary province debuffs that heal automatically.
systems.strengths: Trivially cheap to compute and to understand; manpower-as-pool does create one real strategic rhythm (fight, exhaust, truce, recover) and makes attrition warfare legible. For a map game about armies and borders it is arguably sufficient.
systems.weaknesses: Because people aren't modeled, nothing demographic can matter: no war-generation lost, no refugees, no urbanization, no emigration. The Thirty Years' War can kill a third of Germany in reality; in EU4 a decade later everything is as before. Culture conversion is a mana purchase, not a social process. This is the root reason EU4 economies feel dead: with no consumers there is no internal economy, only tax extraction, so 'economy' collapses into modifier-stacking.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID as an economic foundation, but STEAL the pool pattern for the right subsystems. Our population must be real (we have the 1950 data — it's a core asset): conscription pools, labor supply, and consumer demand should all draw from the same demographic base so guns-vs-butter is a real constraint (the Soviet dilemma of 1941 and of 1980 alike). But EU4-style regenerating pools are the correct abstraction for genuinely pool-like things: trained reserves, officer corps quality, mobilization readiness. The test: if losing it should scar a nation for a generation (people), simulate it; if it recovers on a known timetable (readiness), pool it.

key_takeaways: The Vic2-vs-EU4 verdict: Vic2's emergent pops created strictly better STRATEGIC decisions (long-horizon, indirect, tradeoff-laden — educate now to industrialize in 30 years) while EU4's abstraction created better TACTICAL decisions (legible, fast, comparable) that decayed into solved spreadsheets. The synthesis for our game is asymmetric by ideology: give planned economies EU4-grade direct legibility (you place the steel mill; the sim resists via shortages and gamed targets) and market economies Vic2-grade indirection (you set rates and contracts; firms decide) — the difference in control style IS the economic-systems-competition pillar, not a modifier delta.

Emergence without legibility is wiki homework: Vic2's deepest systems (two-roll promotion, migration weights, capitalist AI) were beloved in principle and reverse-engineered in practice because the UI never explained them. Budget a 'why' inspector for every emergent outcome (why pops emigrated, why firms won't invest, why the plan missed target) as a first-class feature — it is what separates our simulation from Vic2's opacity, and in the planned-economy case, deliberately DEGRADED information (lagged, manager-falsified reports) can itself be the historically authentic challenge.

Never introduce an abstract universal currency generated outside the simulation (EU4 mana, the franchise's most-litigated mistake). Instead use 3-4 capacity currencies the economy itself produces — construction capacity, administrative capacity, scarce specialists (engineers/physicists, which also throttle the nuclear weapons program) — so EU4's five-second decision clarity coexists with Vic2's 'everything comes from the people' causality.

Any autonomous economic actor (capitalists, firms, plant managers) must have published, simple, correct decision logic, and any policy-regime switch must carry multi-year transition costs. Vic2 proved that a broken investor AI plus free policy switching converts an economic simulation into an exploit (government-cycling meta); the same costs, built deliberately, hand us the 1989 systemic-collapse endgame for free.

Vic2's single prestige-ordered world market is the exact anti-pattern for 1950: replace it with two semi-closed trade systems with different internal logics — a price-and-currency dollar bloc (with CoCom-style export controls as a playable weapon) and a negotiated bilateral-barter COMECON bloc — with the nonaligned world as the contested membrane between them. Trade-system architecture becomes influence warfare by other means.

Model the demographic transition — the single biggest thing BOTH games lack and the one our 1950 population data is uniquely positioned to exploit. Birth/death rates responding to urbanization, healthcare, and education make the Third World boom, the baby boom, and Soviet stagnation emerge from play, and food (explicit calorie balances, stockpiles, famine as political catastrophe) becomes the era-defining stake it actually was from the Great Leap Forward to the Green Revolution.

reports.games: Supreme Ruler series (BattleGoat Studios): Supreme Ruler 2020 (2008), Supreme Ruler: Cold War (2011), Supreme Ruler Ultimate (2014, unifies 1936/CW/2020 engines), Supreme Ruler 2030 (2023). Primary sources: SR Cold War official manual (full PDF read), Supreme Ruler wiki, Steam economy guides and discussions, BGForums, contemporary reviews (Mash Those Buttons, GamingLives, Digitally Downloaded). This is the only serious genre attempt at literal per-facility electricity generation in a Cold War grand strategy.

systems.how_it_works: Electricity is one of 11 explicit commodities, produced daily by discrete power-plant facilities: Power-Coal, Power-Petrol, Power-Hydro, Power-Other (tech-gated), Power-Nuclear (tech-gated, consumes uranium). Coal plants produce ~2x the electricity of petroleum plants at no extra manpower cost; hydro needs no fuel input but has worse maintenance cost per MW than coal. Outputs are literal MWh figures per facility. Electricity is consumed by civilians (scaling with population, and sharply with unemployment under ~3%) AND as an input to nearly every other production chain (industrial goods, consumer goods, military goods factories all require it). It cannot be stockpiled: daily surplus is auto-exported to the world market, daily shortfall auto-imported — meaning landlocked New Zealand can happily import electricity from Iceland. 'Improved Power Grid I-IV' techs each boost ALL power output by +50%, and players report electricity balance is nearly impossible before those techs regardless of how many plants you build.
systems.strengths: Electricity as the universal input creates a genuinely felt industrialization bottleneck — every expansion decision routes through 'do I have the power for this?', which is exactly the right Cold War-era question. The coal/oil/hydro/nuclear fuel-mix decision has real texture: fuel logistics (do I mine coal or import it?), maintenance cost per MW, and manpower differ per type. Players consistently name electricity as tied with industrial goods for most important resource — the system succeeds at making energy the spine of the economy.
systems.weaknesses: Three big failures. (1) Tradeable electricity: because it's just commodity #8 on a global market, you can run a fully industrialized nation with zero power plants by importing power across oceans — universally mocked as absurd, and the devs themselves defaulted energy trading off in some configurations. (2) Flat tech multipliers dominate construction: +50% output per grid tech means the interesting decision is research order, not plant siting; pre-tech shortage feels like an unwinnable treadmill ('build more, still never enough'). (3) No grid/transmission at all — a plant in Vladivostok powers Leningrad identically; geography of generation is cosmetic beyond the build-hex supply rating.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT electricity as an explicit commodity and universal industrial input — it's the single best idea in the series and no Paradox game has it. But AVOID the global electricity market: make electricity NON-TRADEABLE and regional. With ~4,600 provinces you can do what SR couldn't: grid zones (province clusters connected by transmission infrastructure you build), where surplus in one zone cannot reach a deficit zone without a line. That instantly makes electrification a spatial planning problem — GOELRO-style — and gives planned economies a signature megaproject verb. Keep the fuel-mix decision (coal vs hydro vs oil vs nuclear) with distinct cost/fuel/lead-time profiles; 1950 nuclear power (Obninsk 1954, Calder Hall 1956) should be a prestige/tech spillover from the weapons program, not an economic play. AVOID flat +50% grid techs; make efficiency gains marginal and let capacity come from building.

systems.how_it_works: Eleven commodities, geographically sourced from real-world deposit data: Agriculture, Fresh Water, Timber, Petroleum, Coal, Ore (metal), Uranium, Electricity, Consumer Goods, Industrial Goods, Military Goods. Raw resources come from location-locked facilities (mines, wells, farms) built on deposit hexes of varying richness ('build on the brightest red hex'). Finished-goods chains: Industrial Goods ← electricity + petroleum + coal + ore; Consumer Goods ← electricity + petroleum + industrial goods + ore (+rubber in some titles); Military Goods ← electricity + industrial goods + ore. The manual is explicit that the world is deliberately NOT balanced — 'not every region has its own large supply of petroleum or coal or even fresh water' — shortage management IS the game. Facility output is modulated by local supply/infrastructure rating (a factory at 50% supply produces ~7.5 of 10 tons — nonlinear) and by population loyalty of the hex.
systems.strengths: Real geographic deposits + deliberately unbalanced world = trade and conquest have authentic motivations; every nation's economic personality emerges from geology. The three-tier chain (raw → industrial goods → consumer/military goods) is shallow enough to hold in your head but deep enough that a coal strike or ore shortage cascades visibly. Supply-rating and loyalty modifiers on output are a quietly brilliant occupation mechanic: conquered land produces far below capacity until supply develops and loyalty (which barely moves) permits — conquest is NOT instant economy absorption.
systems.weaknesses: Eleven parallel commodity bars each needing a production target, a domestic price, an auto-buy and an auto-sell threshold is the core of the 'spreadsheet' accusation — the per-commodity Production Department panel is literally a spreadsheet row per good. Fresh Water as a globally traded commodity is as silly as electricity. AI nations mismanage the chains and collapse (WW2-era sandboxes reportedly end in universal AI economic collapse within 10-15 game years), so the world market degrades into a player-exploitable money pump.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: keep a short commodity list (8-12) with real 1950 geographic deposits — your 4,600-province real-population map is made for this. ADOPT the loyalty/supply output modifiers as your occupation economics. But kill the per-commodity micromanagement surface: in OUR game the planned-vs-market pillar solves this natively — market economies should have most commodity flows priced and cleared automatically (the player sets tariffs/policy, firms respond), while planned economies expose the SR-style manual target-setting AS THE INTENDED EXPERIENCE, with plan targets set per 5-year interval rather than as always-editable sliders. SR accidentally made every country play like Gosplan; make that a Soviet feature, not a universal chore.

systems.domain: Economic planning: treasury, GDP, taxes, world market
systems.how_it_works: Treasury moves by daily Surplus/Deficit = income (taxation across 8 separately settable rates — low/high income, corporate, small business, sales, unemployment, property, pension; domestic commodity sales at player-set prices; diplomacy) minus expenses (facility maintenance, social spending across 8 programs, production costs, research, defense). The player sets the DOMESTIC PRICE of population-consumed goods (food, water, timber, petroleum, electricity, consumer goods) — high prices raise revenue but suppress consumption and approval. GDP/c is a simulated output: taxes lower it, social programs raise it, low unemployment and production raise it; GDP rank drives net migration. Debt is automatic — negative treasury auto-issues bonds; when treasury is negative, unit production, facility construction, market purchases, and treaty payments freeze while raw production, salaries, and social spending continue. World market: auto-buy/auto-sell bands per commodity, or manual bulk orders; withholding surplus escalates the world price. Government type applies economic modifiers — Communism gets cheaper labor and military costs, conscription benefit, but a negative GDP/c drag and lower international approval baseline.
systems.strengths: The department/cabinet structure (State, Finance, Production, Research, Defense — each delegable to an AI minister, lockable per-function or even per-commodity) is a genuinely good answer to complexity: play finance minister today, general tomorrow. Setting domestic prices of essentials is a rare and flavorful lever — it IS the planned-economy experience (bread price riots!). The deficit-freeze rule creates real fiscal brinkmanship. Financial reports laid out by government department make deficits diagnosable.
systems.weaknesses: This is where 'spreadsheet management' lives: 8 tax sliders x 8 social sliders x 11 commodity panels, with feedback loops (GDP↔taxes↔approval↔migration↔unemployment↔inflation) that are opaque enough that even veterans argue about causality on forums. Minister AI adjusts your settings behind your back unless locked. The world market AI is exploitable to the point of farce — documented buy-at-half-price, sell-next-day-at-4x arbitrage that funds entire campaigns. SR2030's tuning shows the fragility: whole-cohort AI deflation/debt spirals, population growth cliffs from modest GDP changes. Communism as 'market economy plus modifiers' is exactly the design our game exists to reject.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID modeling the two systems as one rule set with sign-flipped modifiers — SR proves that reduces the USSR to 'America with cheap labor and a GDP malus'. ADOPT three specific pieces: (1) delegation with per-function lock-out (essential for a game of this scope, and thematically perfect — you ARE appointing a politburo/cabinet); (2) domestic price-setting of essentials as a PLANNED-economy-exclusive lever with riot risk, while market economies get monetary/fiscal levers instead; (3) deficit rules that differ by system — market states face bond markets and credit ratings, planned states face shortage/queue/black-market pressure instead of debt. AVOID a naively arbitrage-able world market: make the 1950 world market thin and bloc-segmented (COMECON vs dollar area) with prices the player can see but not day-trade.

systems.how_it_works: Map is hex-based; each hex holds max 1 complex + 6 facilities. Three complex types gate what can be built: Cities (pre-existing, cannot be player-built — consumer/civic facilities), Industrial Complexes (mines, mills, factories, power plants), Military Bases (fabrication, barracks, airbases). Building on a virgin hex requires constructing the complex first (extra cost, maintenance, and time), so expansion clusters around existing sites.
