Construction consumes money + a steady drain of Industrial Goods daily until completion; build speed scales with local supply rating, and engineering units in the zone accelerate it (and are the only way to open unsupplied territory). Manual explicitly warns that over-building 'can cripple your economy' via simultaneous cash and industrial-goods demand spikes. Scrapping refunds materials; destruction doesn't.
systems.strengths: Construction consuming industrial goods over time (not a lump sum) means an over-ambitious build program starves your OWN factories of inputs — a beautifully self-limiting boom/bust dynamic that mirrors real planned-economy over-investment crises. Complex-gating creates recognizable industrial geography (rust-belt clusters, company towns) instead of uniform sprawl. Engineer units bridging construction and the military supply model is elegant.
systems.weaknesses: Queue management across hundreds of hexes is pure tedium; choosing 'the brightest red hex' is solved play, not a decision. Cities being unbuildable means urbanization — the defining demographic fact of 1950-1990 — doesn't exist. No labor constraint on construction itself beyond money and goods.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT construction as a flow demand on industrial goods (and labor) rather than a point cost — it's the mechanical heart of Five-Year-Plan tension: the player who sets 40 simultaneous projects should watch all of them crawl and consumer goods vanish. ADAPT complex-gating into province specialization at your province scale (a province develops an industrial identity that cheapens further same-type building). AVOID per-hex placement micromanagement: at 4,600 provinces, let the player pick the province and priority; the game sites the plant. And DO model urbanization — rural-to-urban labor transfer should be the growth engine both blocs raced on.

systems.how_it_works: Population per hex from real-world data (as ours is). Population consumes agriculture, water, timber, petroleum, electricity, consumer goods daily. Growth = births/deaths modified by healthcare and family-subsidy spending (healthcare under-funding: life expectancy falls, birthrate drops, death rate rises, immigration falls, emigration rises) plus migration driven by GDP rank (roughly top-50 GDP nations attract net immigration), domestic approval, and infrastructure spending. Labor: employment is emergent from facilities; unemployment below ~3% triggers labor-cost spikes, reduced facility efficiency, and higher electricity demand; rapid industrialization plus maxed social programs can drop unemployment 6%→3% in two game years. Population growth suppresses inflation. In SR2030, high GDP/c abruptly crushes population growth (demographic transition, crudely).
systems.strengths: Labor as a real constraint is rare and valuable: you can build factories you cannot staff, and full employment overheats wages — an actual macro tradeoff, not a mana bar. Migration responding to relative prosperity and approval is exactly the Cold War scoreboard (defections, brain drain, the reason the Wall existed). Social-spending → demographic feedback gives butter a long-run payoff against guns.
systems.weaknesses: The feedbacks are opaque and cliff-prone (SR2030's growth collapses feel like bugs); players optimize by forum lore, not by readable in-game causality. Population is an aggregate scalar per hex — no age structure, so WWII's hollowed-out Soviet male cohort (the defining 1950 demographic fact) is unrepresentable. Migration by GDP-rank table is gamey.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT labor scarcity as a first-class constraint — with real 1950 populations per province this is our comparative advantage; the USSR's story IS labor mobilization (rural reserves → factories) hitting exhaustion by the 1970s, which is a built-in planned-economy late-game brake that needs no scripting. ADAPT migration into a bloc-competition mechanic: emigration pressure from living-standard gaps, with closing the border as an explicit policy carrying legitimacy/influence costs (Berlin 1961 as an emergent player decision). ADD coarse age cohorts (3-5 buckets) — SR shows a scalar is not enough, and the 1950 start makes war-loss demographics load-bearing. AVOID cliff-edge demographic formulas; make every demographic driver inspectable in-UI.

systems.how_it_works: Agriculture is a per-hex facility-produced commodity (Agriculture farms, tech-gated Hydroponics), consumed by population daily and as raw input elsewhere (e.g., biofuels in modern eras); Fresh Water is a separate commodity (Water Works, tech-gated Water Reclamation). Shortfalls are auto-imported at world price; sustained shortage or unaffordable player-set food prices hit domestic approval and reduce military unit efficiency. Standard opening advice for any developing nation: build agriculture/water to self-sufficiency before anything else. Farm output tied to hex suitability from real geography.
systems.strengths: Food self-sufficiency as the mandatory first rung of development gives small/poor nations a distinct early game, and 'food shortage degrades army efficiency' is a clean guns-vs-butter coupling. Water scarcity as a separate lever creates real regional character (Middle East plays differently).
systems.weaknesses: Once self-sufficient, agriculture becomes background noise — no harvest variance, no weather, no collectivization-style policy choices; it's a solved checkbox. Food price-setting exists but has none of the political drama it had historically. Globally traded water is nonsense.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT with policy drama attached: 1950 is the era of collectivization (China 1953-58, Eastern Europe), the Virgin Lands campaign (1954), Great Leap famine (1959-61), and US grain surpluses as a diplomatic weapon (PL-480, 1972 grain sales to USSR). Agriculture should be a POLICY battleground, not a facility count: planned economies choose procurement quotas vs peasant incentives (short-run extraction vs long-run yield), market economies manage surpluses and farm lobbies. ADOPT harvest variance (weather rolls) so grain becomes a recurring crisis input to the influence war — the USSR buying American wheat is a legible humiliation mechanic. Keep water sub-national/non-traded or drop it.

systems.how_it_works: Gated behind the 'Nuclear Weapons Production' research project in a real-world tech tree (research slots = number of Research Centers + 1 per capital; projects cost money and time, adjustable by research budget). Warheads are then fabricated like units, consuming large quantities of money, time, and stockpiled URANIUM (uranium is a mined/traded commodity — no-deposit nations can buy it on the open market and stockpile toward a bomb). Delivery is modeled seriously for 2011: free-fall bombs, then MRBMs/ICBMs (silo, sub, air, surface-launch platform classes; missile size vs platform capacity limits — ICBMs only fit subs and silos), interceptable only by late MDI tech. Use consequences: heavy domestic approval hit, always traceable to source, 'international pariah' status with extreme reactions from all regions. Worldwide DEFCON bar (5→1) tracks superpower tension. Separate Space Race track requires both research milestones AND physical facility construction per stage.
systems.strengths: Tying the bomb to a physical uranium stockpile plus long fabrication time makes proliferation a visible, interdictable industrial process rather than a research-complete popup — you can watch a rival accumulate uranium and act. The platform/size delivery model makes the triad an actual procurement decision. Pariah/traceability consequences at least gesture at the taboo. Space Race requiring facilities, not just tech, is a good pattern.
systems.weaknesses: Anyone with market access can simply BUY uranium toward a bomb — no enrichment step, no safeguards, no espionage visibility mechanics; the hard 90% of a real weapons program (fissile material production) is a market transaction. Deterrence is not modeled — nukes are just big artillery with an approval tax, so the AI either never uses them or uses them senselessly; MAD is manual flavor text, not a system. DEFCON is a passive thermometer, not a lever.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT heavily — this is one of our four pillars and SR gives a skeleton plus a list of what to fix. ADOPT: physical fissile-material pipeline as the pacing spine, but split it properly: uranium ore → enrichment/reactor-plutonium FACILITIES (huge, power-hungry, years to build) → weapons-grade stockpile → warhead fabrication → mating to delivery platforms. The enrichment step is the game: it's detectable by espionage (pillar synergy), it consumes enormous ELECTRICITY (Oak Ridge used ~1% of US power — a literal bridge between our electricity system and the bomb), and it can't be bought on a market. AVOID nukes-as-usable-artillery: usage should be endgame-adjacent, with deterrence/brinkmanship (our DEFCON analogue as a player-escalated ladder with commitment costs) doing the real work. Market uranium purchases should feed civilian reactors under safeguards, with diversion as a detectable espionage event.

systems.domain: Interface & delegation (cross-cutting: what made it 'spreadsheet management')
systems.how_it_works: Five government departments, each a dense panel stack of sliders, per-commodity controls, and reports; cabinet ministers can run any department under 6 assignable priorities, lockable per-function and (in Production) per-commodity; alert-notice feeds down the screen edge categorized by department; financial reports mirror department structure. Reviewers: 'never at any point does the game feel like a game more than a serious simulator'; 'buttons for options are everywhere'; confusion 'more often than not'.
systems.strengths: The delegation architecture is the right idea and ahead of its time — granular lock-outs mean you choose your job and trust ministers with the rest. Department-mirrored financial reporting makes 'why am I broke' answerable. Per-commodity minister locks are exactly how a real leader interacts with an economy.
systems.weaknesses: Delegation was necessary because the raw control surface was unplayable, and the minister AI was bad enough (silently changing your prices/trades; unable to exit crises) that veterans locked everything and ate the spreadsheet anyway. The game presented STATE (200 numbers) instead of DECISIONS (5 tradeoffs); nothing summarized 'what matters today'. That, more than depth itself, is the spreadsheet feel.
systems.lesson_for_1950: The core UX law from this series: simulation depth didn't kill SR — undifferentiated presentation of that depth did. ADOPT competent, characterful delegation from day one (your planners/ministers as named agents whose ideology biases their choices — a Gosplan that over-reports fulfillment IS Cold War flavor). Design the default loop around periodic decision moments (annual budget, five-year plan congress, quarterly market reports) that surface 3-6 tradeoffs, with the full data layer one click deeper for those who want it. If the player must open a per-commodity panel weekly to avoid losing, we've rebuilt SR's failure.

key_takeaways: Electricity as an explicit, universal industrial input is the series' best idea and its execution failure is precise: SR made electricity a globally tradeable, non-storable commodity with no grid. Our version: non-tradeable, produced and consumed within transmission-connected province clusters the player must physically wire together. On a 4,600-province map, electrification becomes THE planned-economy megaproject verb (GOELRO, TVA, rural electrification as influence propaganda) and enrichment plants' gigantic power draw hard-links the electricity system to the nuclear weapons pillar.

SR proves 'communism = capitalism with modifiers' is a dead end — its Communist government type is just cheap labor plus a GDP malus, and every country ends up playing like Gosplan anyway because all 11 commodities need manual targets and prices. Invert this: make SR-style manual target/price-setting the planned economy's EXCLUSIVE and intended interface (with shortage/queue/black-market failure modes instead of debt), and give market economies an auto-clearing economy steered by fiscal/monetary/trade policy (with recession/inflation failure modes). The two rule sets should have different screens, different verbs, and different ways to die.

Construction as a continuous flow demand on industrial goods (SR's model) rather than a lump-sum cost is the single mechanic that makes over-investment crises emergent: launch too many simultaneous projects and everything crawls while consumer goods vanish — the authentic Five-Year-Plan failure mode, no scripting required. Adopt it, and pair it with SR's other underrated rule: negative treasury freezes construction and purchases but not wages and social spending, creating real fiscal brinkmanship.

Labor, not money, should be the binding constraint. SR's sub-3%-unemployment wage spiral and staffed-facility model is rare in the genre and matches the actual Soviet growth story: extensive growth by moving peasants into factories, then stagnation when the rural reserve runs dry — a built-in, unscripted late-game brake on planned economies. With real 1950 populations we can do this properly, and migration (defection, brain drain, closing borders at legitimacy cost) turns the same system into influence-war scoreboard.

For nuclear weapons, steal SR's skeleton (physical uranium stockpile, long fabrication, platform-limited delivery, pariah consequences) but insert the step SR skipped: enrichment/plutonium facilities. That single addition makes proliferation slow, capital-intensive, electricity-hungry, and — crucially — espionage-detectable, wiring three of our four pillars together; and never model warheads as usable artillery, because SR shows that path yields AIs that either ignore nukes or use them randomly, with MAD existing only in the manual.

The 'spreadsheet game' verdict on SR was earned by presentation, not depth: it showed 200 numbers of state instead of a handful of decisions, and its minister AI was too incompetent to trust with the difference. Budget as much design effort for the decision-surfacing layer (periodic plan congresses/budget moments presenting 3-6 real tradeoffs, ministers as characterful, ideologically biased agents) as for the simulation itself — depth players never lose to un-surfaced numbers is depth that reviews as jank.

reports.games: Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic (3Division, 1.0 in 2024 after 5 years Early Access) — primary; Factorio (Wube) — secondary comparison

systems.how_it_works: W&R's signature system. Every building can be built two ways: (1) instant-ish 'auto-build' paid in rubles or dollars (expensive foreign-currency shortcut), or (2) physical construction: a Construction Office dispatches excavators, bulldozers, cranes, and trucks through explicit stages — ground leveling, footings (gravel/concrete), structure (concrete panels or bricks + steel), then boards, mechanical components (produced 15t from 22t steel per factory-day), and finally workers physically present on site to do labor. Materials must be hauled from storage or factories by actual vehicles over actual roads. A road that isn't built yet means the crane can't reach the site. Construction time is emergent from logistics throughput, not a fixed timer.
systems.strengths: The money-build vs self-build duality IS the planned-economy fantasy: early game you spend scarce hard currency, late game a mature construction sector builds 'for free' from domestic steel and cement. Players adore the moment their republic becomes materially self-sufficient — it's the game's core progression arc. Construction competes with industry and export for the same steel/concrete, creating genuine planning tradeoffs. Infrastructure has real opportunity cost and real lead time.
systems.weaknesses: Reviewers consistently call it the point where the game 'turns into a screensaver': once construction offices are set up, you queue buildings and wait, with little decision density. Per-site vehicle micromanagement is fiddly; terrain-flatness and rotation placement restrictions add tedium unrelated to strategy. No partial functionality — a building is 0% useful until 100% done.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT, aggressively abstracted. At country scale (4,600 provinces), keep the two deep truths: (a) construction consumes real materials (steel, cement, machinery) drawn from the same national balance as everything else, and (b) construction speed is bounded by a national/regional 'construction capacity' pool (the Construction Office, abstracted) plus local labor. Never simulate vehicles or stages. The planned economy should get W&R's arc explicitly: USSR player can build with materials-in-kind and conscripted labor (fast if balances allow, zero hard currency), while market economies build via firms responding to prices and financing. Avoid: instant cash-build as a universal escape valve — gate it as 'imports' costing hard currency, which for the USSR is the strategically scarce resource.

systems.how_it_works: W&R: every commodity is a tonnage with explicit conversion recipes (e.g., 22t steel → 15t mechanical components per factory per day; uranium mine yields 0.75t ore per worker per workday). Output scales with workers present, their education, and loyalty-driven productivity. Chains are long: ore → steel mill (needs coal) → mech. components → construction/vehicles. Factorio: pure ratio math (items/sec), no workers, and its genius is the bottleneck loop — players iteratively find the binding constraint (Factorio community wisdom: factories 'choking at blue science almost always lack supply density in the tier before, not at blue itself') and expand upstream.
systems.strengths: Explicit chains make shortages legible and diagnosable — the player can trace 'no tractors because no steel because no coal because the rail line is saturated.' Factorio proves that bottleneck-hunting is intrinsically compulsive gameplay; W&R proves it survives adding labor as an input. Worker education/loyalty as productivity multipliers ties industry to the social simulation.
systems.weaknesses: W&R chains demand per-factory placement and per-route logistics that would be lethal at country scale. Factorio's ratios are solvable — optimal blueprints exist, and copy-paste kills decision-making. Both games have effectively infinite demand (export/science), so 'more is always better' with no overproduction penalty — the opposite of real planned economies, whose defining pathology was misallocation, not underproduction.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the explicit chain, at maybe 25–40 commodities, resolved at province/region level as flow balances (tons/month), not factories on a map — Gosplan's material-balance planning was literally this spreadsheet, so the mechanic is also the historical simulation. The player-facing planned-economy loop should be Factorio's bottleneck hunt wearing a Five-Year-Plan costume: set output targets, watch the balance sheet reveal the binding constraint, reallocate. Critically, ADD what both games lack: overproduction and misallocation costs (storage, spoilage, quality decay, plan-fulfillment lying by regional managers) so the planned economy has its authentic failure mode, not just 'slow Factorio.'

systems.how_it_works: W&R models generation → transmission → distribution as separate layers: power plants (coal/oil consume physically delivered fuel; nuclear consumes fabricated fuel, single reactor >4,500 MWh output, the strongest plant in game), high-voltage lines, transformers (1 high-voltage in → 6 medium out), and substations that each distribute max 2.5 MW to buildings within 325m. Overloaded grids cause flickering, then brownouts; unpowered factories stop. Power switches interconnect lines, including priority switches. Nuclear requires the full domestic fuel chain: uranium mine → processing (uranium oxide) → conversion (UF6, transportable only in radiation-shielded containers) → fuel fabrication → reactor.
systems.strengths: Electricity as a hard dependency creates cascading-failure drama players remember: a coal train delayed → power plant dark → whole city stops. The fuel-supply chain makes nuclear power a late-game industrial achievement, not a button. Grid topology (substation radius, transformer fan-out) creates spatial planning puzzles.
systems.weaknesses: Line-and-substation topology is city-scale busywork; at country scale it's noise. W&R nuclear is just 'big power plant' — no waste, no meltdown risk, no dual-use tension, wasting the theme. Grid failures in W&R punish via crisis micromanagement rather than strategic choice.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT to regional grid pools: each region has generation capacity (by plant type, each consuming fuel from the national balance) and demand from industry + population; interconnection capacity between regions is a buildable strategic asset (GOELRO/rural-electrification as a plan goal, a real 1950s prestige metric). Keep the cascading dependency: power deficit → rationing choice (households vs factories vs the enrichment plant), which is a great planned-economy decision. Nuclear POWER should share infrastructure with the weapons program (see below) — reactors produce plutonium as a byproduct, making 'Atoms for Peace' a real dual-use choice. Avoid substations, lines, per-plant placement.

systems.how_it_works: W&R simulates every citizen individually from childhood to death: needs (food, clothing, alcohol, electronics, healthcare, culture, sport, education), happiness, and a separate LOYALTY stat. Loyalty rises via monuments (up to ~40%), radio/TV propaganda (which can backfire if broadcasting stations are unstaffed/mismanaged), and well-run orphanages; it falls from unmet needs, crime, and forced relocation. High loyalty = higher workplace productivity AND tolerance of hardship; unhappy citizens with low loyalty emigrate across the border, permanently draining the labor force. Education levels gate which jobs citizens can fill.
systems.strengths: Loyalty-as-substitute-for-consumption is the single most transferable mechanic in the game: players genuinely choose between making people materially satisfied and making them ideologically committed, and propaganda as a lever with failure modes is superb. Emigration as the punishment for failure (rather than abstract unrest) is visceral and historically resonant — it's literally why the Berlin Wall exists. Labor as the universal scarce input (not money) is what makes the economy feel planned.
systems.weaknesses: Per-citizen agent simulation caps the game at tens of thousands of people — utterly non-scalable to a country of 180M. Reviewers note all needs hit at once with 'no room to start humble,' front-loading complexity. Happiness/loyalty interactions are opaque and were rebalanced repeatedly through EA.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the loyalty/consumption/emigration triangle; REBUILD the substrate as demographic cohorts per province (your 4,600 provinces with real 1950 pop are perfect for this: age bands × education × urban/rural, aging yearly). The planned economy's core dial should be exactly W&R's: divert output from consumer goods to heavy industry/military and cover the gap with propaganda and coercion — with rising instability and emigration pressure (defection, brain drain, Berlin 1953/Hungary 1956 events) as the interest on that debt. Border control (walls, exit visas) should be a buildable but internationally costly answer, feeding your influence-warfare pillar. Education as a slow investment that gates industrial and nuclear capacity transfers directly.

systems.how_it_works: W&R: crops grow on placed fields with seasons and harvest windows; tractors sow, harvesters reap (weather-sensitive), fertilizer (solid or liquid, from the chemical chain) boosts yield; crops go to silos, then a food factory (roughly 51 large fields ≈ 245 ha to saturate one food factory), then trucks distribute food to grocery stores/shopping centers where citizens physically shop. Livestock farms consume crops to make meat; distilleries make alcohol (a citizen need). A break anywhere — no fuel for harvesters, no trucks, no shop stock — means citizens go hungry, tanking happiness then triggering emigration.
systems.strengths: Field-to-store as a chain means famine is a logistics failure you caused and can trace, not an RNG event. Seasonality creates a real annual rhythm (harvest surge, winter drawdown) that rewards storage planning. Fertilizer linking the chemical industry to food output is a smart cross-chain dependency.
systems.weaknesses: Field placement and harvest micromanagement is the most tedious part of W&R at even city scale. The chain's length means new players starve cities through unintuitive breaks (food in the silo, nobody delivering). No soil, no bad-harvest variance worth planning around, no collectivization politics — the most interesting Soviet agricultural questions are absent.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT to province-level agriculture: each province has arable land, rural labor cohort, mechanization level (tractors from YOUR industry), and fertilizer input → seasonal food output with weather variance. Keep the chain shape (production → procurement/transport → urban distribution) because Soviet famines were procurement failures, not just crop failures — grain requisition quotas as a player-set slider (take too much → rural starvation and loyalty collapse; too little → cities starve) is a mechanic no other strategy game does and fits 1950 (Ukraine 1946-47 was three years prior). ADD collectivization state and virgin-lands-style campaigns as plan decisions with yield/loyalty tradeoffs. AVOID fields, vehicles, and shops entirely.

systems.how_it_works: W&R has ~40+ physical commodities (coal, ores, steel, crops, fabric, clothes, chemicals, fuel, UF6...) and its iron rule: nothing teleports. Every ton moves by truck, train, ship, conveyor, pipeline, or forklift, through storages with capacity, loaded/unloaded at real speeds. Distribution offices (researched later) partially automate routing. Factorio is the same rule with belts/bots and infinite ore patches that deplete per-tile.
systems.strengths: The no-teleport rule is why both games feel true: transport capacity becomes a first-class strategic constraint, and infrastructure investment has visible payoff. Resource geography (mines are where they are) forces long-haul corridors — very Trans-Siberian.
systems.weaknesses: Per-vehicle simulation is the #1 source of W&R's tedium per reviews ('hundreds of objects... adjustment consumes real time'; 'crisis-management instead of pre-planning'). It caps map scale and would be catastrophic at country scale. Global market in W&R has shifting prices but infinite depth — export anything forever, which erases scarcity strategy.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT to a capacitated flow network: provinces hold deposits (finite where it matters — uranium!), and rail/port/pipeline links have tonnage capacity per month; the game solves flows, the player builds capacity and sets priorities. Keep the strategic consequence (interdictable, bombable, embargo-able corridors — feeds your espionage/brinkmanship pillars: sabotage a rail hub, blockade Berlin) without any vehicle existing. Resource geography from real 1950 data (Donbas coal, Baku oil, Urals metallurgy) should make provinces genuinely unequal and worth influencing/fighting over. Make foreign trade finite and political: quotas, embargoes (CoCom export controls on the USSR are period-perfect), not an infinite-depth market.

systems.how_it_works: Neither game models weapons programs, but both model the industrial spine one needs. W&R: uranium mine (0.75 t ore/worker/day) → processing plant (ore → uranium oxide/yellowcake) → conversion plant (→ UF6, movable only in shielded containers) → fuel fabrication → reactor; a long, expensive, education-hungry chain. Factorio: uranium ore processing yields U-235 at only 0.7% probability vs 99.3% U-238, making enrichment a slow stochastic grind until the Kovarex enrichment process (needs a 40-unit U-235 stockpile to bootstrap) turns it exponential; the atomic bomb then costs 30 U-235 each and trivializes combat.
systems.strengths: Both prove enrichment-as-scarcity-bottleneck is compelling: Factorio's 0.7% yield makes the first bomb an event players plan toward for hours, and Kovarex is a beloved 'program breakthrough' moment. W&R's chain shows how many distinct facilities, educated workers, and support industries sit under 'we have nuclear capability' — the capability IS the industrial base.
systems.weaknesses: W&R wastes the chain on power only — no weapons, no dual-use tension, no secrecy. Factorio's bomb is a win-more item with no strategic layer. Neither models the real constraints: scientist talent pools, espionage-acquired design knowledge, test detection.
systems.lesson_for_1950: BUILD THIS YOURSELVES — it's your pillar and no one has done it as an industrial chain. Model the weapons program as: finite uranium provinces (Joachimsthal, Fergana, Congo, Canada — instant geopolitical objects) → milling → conversion → ENRICHMENT CAPACITY (gaseous diffusion plants: enormous, years to build, and consuming several percent of national ELECTRICITY — Oak Ridge's K-25 famously rivaled whole cities; this welds the weapons program to your power system) → weapons-grade stockpile in kg → device design (science + espionage: the USSR's 1949 bomb was a Fat Man copy) → tests (detectable, prestige/terror effects) → stockpile + delivery systems. Offer the plutonium route (reactors + reprocessing, dual-use with civilian power) vs HEU route as a real tradeoff. Factorio's lesson: make the FIRST bomb a long, legible, milestone-driven grind; W&R's lesson: make sustained arsenal growth an industrial-base question, so economic systems competition literally determines who wins the arms race.

systems.how_it_works: W&R's most radical design choice: the internal economy has NO money. Wages, prices, and profits don't exist domestically — only resource stocks, flows, workers, and needs. Rubles and dollars exist solely as foreign exchange, earned by physically hauling goods to border customs houses (Soviet bloc pays rubles, NATO pays dollars) and spent on imports and auto-builds; global market prices drift every few days. The player is Gosplan: success is measured in material balances and met needs, not GDP. Realistic mode removes even starting cash cushions.
systems.strengths: This is the proof-of-concept your game needs: a moneyless in-kind economy is playable, legible, and fun — arguably MORE fun than budget-based city builders because every decision is about real stuff. The two-currency/two-bloc structure creates authentic Cold War texture: exporting to NATO for dollars to buy Western machine tools while staying in the ruble zone politically. Hard-currency hunger as the planned economy's Achilles heel emerges naturally.
systems.weaknesses: The player is a perfect, incorruptible, all-seeing planner — no principal-agent problem, no false reporting, no soft budget constraints, no shortage-hoarding by enterprises. Real planned economies failed on information and incentives, and W&R models neither, so it's an argument that planning works great if you're a competent god. Also no counterpart simulation of a market economy to compete against.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the moneyless-internal/forex-external structure wholesale for the socialist bloc — it's correct, it's differentiating, and W&R proves it plays. Then go where W&R doesn't: (1) the player sets plan TARGETS and imperfect regional apparatchiks execute, with fulfillment reports that can be inflated (purges/inspections as the espionage-flavored audit mechanic); (2) market economies get a genuinely different ruleset — firms, prices, business cycles, and indirect levers (rates, tariffs, procurement) so the two systems are asymmetric rule sets, not skins; (3) hard currency (and gold) as the USSR's binding external constraint, with grain-for-gold and resource exports as painful levers. The systems-competition scoreboard should compare consumer standard of living vs heavy-industry/military output — the exact tradeoff each side propagandized.

key_takeaways: W&R's moneyless internal economy is the existence proof your economic-competition pillar needs: a planned economy tracked purely in material balances, workers, and needs — with rubles/dollars only as foreign exchange — is playable and fun. Adopt that structure for the socialist bloc, then add the two things W&R omits because the player is a perfect planner: imperfect subordinate execution (inflated fulfillment reports, audits, purges) and asymmetric market-economy rules on the other side.

The loyalty/consumption/emigration triangle is the best social mechanic to steal: propaganda and monuments substitute for consumer goods but accrue instability debt, and the failure state is people physically leaving. At your scale, rebuild it on demographic cohorts per province (your 4,600 provinces with real 1950 population are ideal), and make border control a buildable answer with international-reputation cost — the Berlin Wall as an emergent player decision.

Nothing W&R does at object level survives country scale — vehicles, fields, substations, construction stages are its tedium engine even at city scale per reviewers ('turns into a screensaver', 'crisis-management instead of pre-planning'). What scales is the RULE underneath each: construction consumes materials from the national balance and bounded capacity; power is regional generation/demand pools with fuel dependencies; logistics is a capacitated rail/port network. Keep every dependency, delete every entity.

Factorio's core loop — find the binding constraint, expand upstream, repeat — is the Five-Year Plan as gameplay; Gosplan's material-balance method was literally this. Your planning UI should be a legible national balance sheet that makes the current bottleneck diagnosable in seconds. But add what both games lack: overproduction, spoilage, and misallocation costs, so the planned economy has its authentic failure mode (wrong stuff) rather than just being slow Factorio (not enough stuff).

Build the nuclear weapons program as an industrial chain, not a research bar — neither game does it and it's your biggest open design space. Finite uranium geography → conversion → enrichment plants that devour years of construction and a visible percent of national electricity (welding the bomb to your power and construction systems) → kg of fissile material → espionage-acceleratable design → detectable tests. Plutonium-via-reactors vs HEU-via-diffusion gives a real dual-use choice, and arsenal growth becomes a direct readout of economic-system performance — which is the actual thesis of the Cold War.

Make food a procurement chain, not a farming sim: province agriculture (land × rural labor × mechanization × fertilizer × weather) feeding a player-set state requisition quota, where taking too much starves the countryside and taking too little starves the cities. W&R proves chain-shaped famine (traceable to your own logistics/allocation choice) beats RNG famine; province-level procurement politics is the historically correct and mechanically novel version of it.

reports.games: Terminal Conflict (Strategy Mill, 2020); Crisis in the Kremlin (1991 original + Kremlingames 2017 remake + Crisis in the Kremlin: The Cold War, 2022); Ostalgie: The Berlin Wall (Kremlingames, 2018); China: Mao's Legacy (Kremlingames, 2019); Suzerain (Torpor Games, 2020, incl. Kingdom of Rizia DLC); Twilight Struggle (GMT, 2005 / digital 2016). Common thread: all are tiny-team games that replace production simulation with POLITICAL-ECONOMIC feedback loops — and the loops, not the production math, are what players praise in reviews.

systems.how_it_works: Crisis in the Kremlin (1991/2017): annual budget allocated across ~10 lines (heavy industry, light industry, agriculture, MIC, state apparatus, KGB, welfare); each sector's health computed mostly separately with weak cross-links; the 'state mechanism' line must run 40-100 points above other lines or corruption climbs. CitK: The Cold War adds the killer feature: at ~40% corruption, the statistics the PLAYER sees are falsified — local officials report fake numbers, so your dashboard lies to you until you invest in computerization (OGAS network tech) to shorten the reporting chain. China: Mao's Legacy: three sector stocks (Industry starts at 35, Agriculture, Services) fed by per-yuan investment with hard marginal-yield breakpoints (+0.2 per ¥ up to 7¥ for industry, +0.1 above; agriculture breakpoint 3¥, services 4¥); budget income = +0.1¥ per 5.0 industry etc., minus 0.1¥ per point of corruption; the Five-Year Plan is a pick-one-sector focus that costs -0.1 science/day unless you pick Science; a discrete economy-type selector (Planned / State Capitalism / Birdcage / Market-with-minimum-regulation) rescales corruption generation. Suzerain: the entire treasury is ~8 discrete budget tokens per term spent on named ministries/projects; debt below -9 by turn 9 hard-triggers a debt crisis that locks economic progression.
systems.strengths: Chunky integer budgets (Suzerain, Mao) make every point an agonizing, nameable choice — community guides obsess over single-token decisions. The guns-vs-butter slider tension is immediately legible. Falsified statistics is the single best planned-economy mechanic in the entire niche: it turns 'corruption' from a stat drain into an epistemic problem — you are Gosplan and you cannot trust your own reports. Economy-type as a discrete regime selector (not a slider) makes 'planned vs market' feel like changing rule sets.
systems.weaknesses: Formulas are invisible in-game (all three Kremlingames titles required community datamining to be playable); optimal slider settings are solved once and copy-pasted every run; money buys abstract 'sector points' directly with no physical intermediates, no time-to-build, no capital goods; the five-year plan degenerates into a passive buff pick with zero commitment or accountability; CitK reviews repeatedly cite 'no causal relation between decisions and outcomes' as the top complaint.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: use discrete, chunky plan allocations (not continuous sliders) for the planned bloc, but bind them to physical outputs (tons of steel, kWh, grain) flowing through provinces. Make the Five-Year Plan a BINDING public commitment: you set targets, the world sees them, shortfall costs legitimacy and fulfillment can be falsified by your own apparatus — adopt the falsified-statistics mechanic wholesale as the planned economy's signature epistemic weakness (and make espionage able to steal the REAL numbers, linking to our espionage pillar). Publish the formulas in-UI; Kremlingames' opacity is their most-cited flaw and it is free to avoid.

systems.how_it_works: China: Mao's Legacy imposes diminishing returns on crash investment: marginal yield halves past per-turn soft caps; sector stocks above thresholds (industry >39.9) suffer a -1.2 decay penalty unless propped by research and complementary sectors; imbalance (services far above industry+agriculture) generates corruption; and a campaign deadline — by 1980, industry+agriculture+services minus corruption must exceed 150 — or you take a permanent 'backward economy' modifier. CitK: The Cold War similarly makes light industry decay if starved while heavy-industry spending 'ramps up in cost' with unguaranteed spillover.
systems.strengths: Soft caps and cross-sector balance requirements are effective anti-snowball devices: you cannot just firehose money into heavy industry, which is exactly the correct Stalinist temptation to punish. The 1980 deadline gives the whole economy game an arc and stakes.
systems.weaknesses: All thresholds are hidden (the -1.2 decay above 39.9 is pure guide-lore); penalties feel arbitrary rather than diegetic; zero spatial dimension — 'Industry 38.2' is a single national float, so there is nothing to build anywhere.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: diminishing returns on crash industrialization is the right core idea — real command economies were constrained by absorptive capacity, not money. But express it diegetically and LOCALLY: with 4,600 provinces, cap construction throughput per province by cement, skilled labor, and electricity available there, visible in the UI. 'You can order ten steel mills in the Urals but only pour two foundations a year' is the same math as Mao's Legacy's hidden curve breaks, except the player can see, plan around, and invest against it.

systems.domain: agriculture & food / consumer goods vs heavy industry
systems.how_it_works: CitK: light industry (consumer goods) stagnates then decays without continuous input; deficits raise discontent and feed a black market. Mao's Legacy: the agricultural SYSTEM is a structural choice — People's Communes vs Family Contracts vs Private Farming — each a different rule set for food output, ideology drift, and social metrics; a living-standard floor (<48.7) bleeds stability continuously. Ostalgie's masterstroke is 'Westalgia': consumer dissatisfaction measured not against an absolute threshold but against the visible standard of living of the WEST — driven by media exposure, border regime, and your political system, and it drives emigration and unrest; successful reform with maintained control makes Westalgia decline.
systems.strengths: Westalgia is the best consumer-goods mechanic in the niche because it captures the actual Cold War mechanism: the USSR didn't lose because people starved, it lost because East Germans could watch West German TV. Structural farm-system choices (communes vs family plots) create dramatically different playthroughs where a slider never would. The heavy-vs-light tension is the emotional core of all three Kremlingames titles.
systems.weaknesses: Food is usually a threshold-annoyance, not a system: no harvest variance, no weather, no procurement/price-scissors dynamics; players learn the one safe reform sequence and repeat it; consumer goods are a single aggregate with no distinction between bread, shoes, and televisions.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT relative deprivation as the consumer-satisfaction metric: score each country's living standard against the OTHER BLOC's visible standard, modulated by information penetration (radio/TV/border porosity) — this natively fuses our economy and influence-warfare pillars, and jamming/propaganda become economic policy tools. ADOPT agrarian organization as a per-country rules-set choice (collectivization level) with distinct output/variance/political profiles — a 1950 start makes collectivization drives, the Virgin Lands campaign, and the Great Leap live, high-variance player decisions rather than backstory. Add harvest variance: planned economies should fear the weather.

systems.how_it_works: Ostalgie: you buy named enterprises and modernizations (microelectronics plant, consumer-goods works, Trabant modernization) as one-off purchases from the budget with flat ongoing effects; Western loans or Soviet subsidy fund them. Suzerain: infrastructure and institutions (universities, plants, agencies) are one-click funded decisions costing 1-2 of your ~8 budget tokens, whose payoff arrives several turns later as narrative events and stat shifts. Nothing in any of these games is placed on a map, nothing takes variable time, nothing can fail mid-construction.
systems.strengths: Named projects punch massively above their weight in memorability: players write AARs about 'my microelectronics gamble,' never about generic building queue #47. Delayed payoff creates anticipation and lets a tiny content budget deliver drama. Suzerain proves 8 tokens of budget can carry an entire game's economic decision-making if every spend is a named commitment.
systems.weaknesses: No opportunity-cost texture beyond the money itself; completion is instant or timerless; projects can't run over budget, be sabotaged, or be cancelled at political cost — which discards most of what made real Soviet megaprojects dramatic.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: layer named Great Projects (Volga-Don Canal, Magnitogorsk expansion, Aswan Dam bids, Interstate Highway System) on top of generic province construction. Great Projects get: map placement, multi-year timelines, cost-overrun risk, espionage/sabotage vulnerability, and an influence-warfare payout on completion (prestige broadcast to the Third World). Foreign-funded projects (our Aswan moment) should be THE contested currency of influence warfare. Generic construction handles volume; named projects handle memory.

systems.domain: population & growth (emigration as the active variable)
systems.how_it_works: Terminal Conflict reduces population to 'citizens,' one of five currencies (finance, citizens, elites, military, government) earned via focus bonuses and spent on actions — no demographics at all. Ostalgie makes population ACT: emigration pressure is a function of Westalgia, living standards, repression, and the border regime (open vs closed); outflow drains the economy and legitimacy, and the Wall itself is thereby a mechanic with diplomatic costs, not scenery. No game in the set models natural growth, cohorts, or urbanization.
systems.strengths: Emigration-as-verdict is elegant and cheap: the population votes with its feet, automatically converting economic failure into demographic loss and propaganda humiliation. The border-regime dial (open/closed/shoot-to-kill) is a real decision with costs on every axis.
systems.weaknesses: Population is otherwise inert background; Terminal Conflict's 'citizens as currency' is legible but produces zero Cold War flavor.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT emigration/defection flows as a first-class system: with real 1950 province populations, model refugee flows (pre-Wall Berlin drain, Hungary '56 exodus, Cuban boatlifts) responding to the living-standard gap and border openness, moving actual population between our provinces. Defectors should also carry espionage value (scientists, pilots). Keep natural growth as slow background cohort math — the drama is in movement, not fertility. This is a bridge between economy, influence, and espionage pillars that no big grand strategy game executes well.

systems.how_it_works: Ostalgie runs socialist states on effectively two monies: the domestic budget and hard currency — earned via exports and the Soviet-subsidized oil relationship, spent on Western technology imports, consumer-goods imports to suppress Westalgia, and debt service; Western credits (FRG loans to the GDR) come with political strings, and losing Soviet subsidies as the USSR reforms is a scripted noose. Suzerain: foreign loans carry explicit sovereignty concessions, and the -9 debt threshold hard-locks your economy into crisis. Mao's Legacy stays single-currency but prices politician ideology into budget income (liberal premiers generate more revenue).
systems.strengths: Dual currency is the highest-value planned-economy abstraction in the niche: it explains in one mechanic why a superpower with endless steel cannot buy grain or computers. Loans-with-strings converts finance into influence warfare automatically. Players consistently cite the hard-currency squeeze as Ostalgie's tensest system.
systems.weaknesses: Prices are static — no oil-shock or grain-price dynamics except scripted events; trade partners are menu items, not agents; the resource side (what physically backs exports) is hand-waved.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT dual currency for the planned bloc: soft domestic money (rubles — always sufficient, buys only domestic capacity) vs hard currency (dollars/gold — scarce, buys Western tech, grain, and influence). Hard-currency earners — gold mines, oil, arms exports, and in the 1950s ironically grain — become strategic map assets. Western credit lines are a lever the market bloc PLAYER extends or withdraws (embargoes, CoCom tech controls) as economic warfare. This one mechanic delivers more 'planned vs market as different rule sets' than any production-chain detail, at trivial implementation cost.

systems.how_it_works: Terminal Conflict: the tech tree is almost entirely nuclear (warhead production-rate bonuses, delivery upgrades, SLBMs becoming decisive mid-game); each focus round both players simultaneously declare 'arms race' or 'disarmament' posture — matching postures cheapen military ops or place influence, opposed postures create live warzones; falling behind the arms race emboldens the opponent's aggression; a Doomsday Clock tracks escalation. Twilight Struggle: NO arsenals exist at all — only a shared DEFCON track 5→1: coups in battlegrounds degrade DEFCON, current DEFCON gates which regions allow coups/realignments, each turn you must meet a military-ops quota equal to current DEFCON or lose VP, and whoever CAUSES DEFCON 1 instantly loses. Suzerain: Rizia treats a nuclear program as a multi-year funded royal project with diplomatic fallout. None of the games model the program's physical substance (fissile material, test sites, delivery triad).
systems.strengths: Twilight Struggle proves you need zero warhead counts for terrifying brinkmanship: a shared escalation ladder plus 'the one who triggers armageddon loses' inverts incentives brilliantly — expert players deliberately drive DEFCON to 2 to handcuff the opponent's entire turn (coup lockout), weaponizing risk itself. Terminal Conflict's simultaneous posture declaration is a clean, tense arms-race minigame; its 'lagging deterrence emboldens the enemy' rule makes the arsenal matter without ever firing.
systems.weaknesses: TS's DEFCON is gamey at the edges (trap cards that force opponent-triggered war feel like gotchas); TC's nuke tech is a monotone treadmill — always worth buying, few real choices; treating the arsenal as a pure abstract score forfeits the rich 1950s program story (test detection, spies stealing designs, H-bomb decision) that our espionage pillar wants.
systems.lesson_for_1950: SPLIT THE SYSTEM IN TWO. Layer 1 — the program: model it concretely for a 1950 start (uranium supply, separation plants as constructible sites, test events detectable by rival seismology/fallout sampling, designs stealable by spies); this is where construction, resources, and espionage meet. Layer 2 — use-risk: adopt a TS-style shared escalation ladder where escalatory acts degrade it, the current level gates available aggression worldwide, and BLAME for crossing thresholds is the resource at stake — the side judged responsible for escalation bleeds world opinion (influence pillar). Deterrence math (TC's 'lagging arsenal emboldens the rival') sets what escalation options each side can credibly threaten. Never model nuclear war as a damage calculation to win; model it as a blame game everyone loses.

systems.how_it_works: Essentially absent across all six games: no grid, no generation capacity, no power as an industrial input. Civilian nuclear appears only as scripted disaster events (Chernobyl in Kremlingames titles) or as a fundable prestige project (Rizia). The one gem: CitK: The Cold War features OGAS — the Soviet nationwide computer network — as a multi-year transformative goal (3+ years of investment) that fixes the planned economy's information problem and serves as an alternate victory condition.
systems.strengths: OGAS-as-goal shows there is player appetite for utopian infrastructure endgames that CHANGE THE RULES of your economy type rather than just adding output.
systems.weaknesses: The absence means none of these games can represent electrification as the core socialist promise ('Communism is Soviet power plus electrification of the whole country') or Atoms for Peace as influence competition.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT into open design space — no competitor occupies it. Make electricity a real province-level input gating industrial throughput (ties into the absorptive-capacity system above), make electrification RATE a headline plan target and propaganda number for the planned bloc, and make civilian nuclear (Obninsk 1954, Calder Hall 1956, Atoms for Peace) a prestige-and-influence race distinct from the weapons program but sharing its fissile-material base — forcing a genuine plutonium-for-bombs vs power-and-prestige allocation choice.

key_takeaways: The best small-game abstractions price POLITICS into economics, not production into spreadsheets: falsified plan statistics (CitK: The Cold War), Westalgia/relative deprivation (Ostalgie), and loans-with-strings (Ostalgie, Suzerain) each cost almost nothing to implement and generate more Cold War texture than any production chain. Steal the feedback distortions, not the production math.

Dual currency — soft domestic money vs scarce hard currency — is the single highest-leverage mechanic for making planned economies a genuinely different rule set: it explains why the steel superpower can't buy grain, makes gold/oil/arms-exports strategic map assets, and hands the market bloc an economic-warfare lever (credit, CoCom embargoes) for free.

Chunky discrete allocations and NAMED projects beat continuous sliders every time: players remember 'I gambled on the microelectronics plant,' never 'I set light industry to 62%.' Headline construction with map-placed Great Projects that have timelines, overrun risk, sabotage vulnerability, and influence payouts; let generic queues handle volume underneath.

Separate 'having nukes' from 'risking nukes': model the weapons program physically (uranium, separation plants, detectable tests — espionage's favorite target in 1950) but model brinkmanship as a Twilight-Struggle-style shared escalation ladder where blame for escalating is the stake and the side that triggers catastrophe loses. Risk itself becomes a weapon players deliberately wield — TS's deepest lesson.

Command economies need absorptive-capacity limits as their anti-snowball (Mao's Legacy's diminishing returns are correct), but surface them diegetically as visible local bottlenecks — cement, skilled labor, electricity per province — never as hidden curve breaks; every Kremlingames title is dragged down in reviews by formula opacity, a flaw that costs nothing to avoid.

Population should act, not just grow: emigration and defection flows responding to living-standard gaps and border regimes (Ostalgie) convert economic failure directly into demographic loss, propaganda humiliation, and espionage windfalls — with real 1950 province populations, refugee flows (Berlin drain, Hungary '56) are our cheapest unique bridge between the economy, influence, and espionage pillars.

reports.games: Civilization IV, Civilization V, Civilization VI (+ Gathering Storm), Millennia, Old World

systems.how_it_works: One production currency ('hammers'/cogs) per city, spent on exactly one item at a time from a queue. Cost is a fixed sticker price (e.g. Civ VI Manhattan Project = 1000 production); progress = city production/turn, with overflow carrying to the next item (Civ IV overflow is famously exploitable via whip timing). Acceleration levers: Civ IV Slavery civic converts 1 population into 30 hammers (+1 unhappiness per whip event regardless of size); Civ V/VI let you buy items outright with gold (~4x the hammer cost) or faith; Civ VI policy cards give targeted +100% toward unit/wonder classes; forest chops dump lump-sum production. Old World breaks the single currency into three parallel ones — Growth (civilian units), Training (military), Civics (projects/specialists) — which accumulate as stockpiles you can also spend directly, and gates all actions behind a shared per-turn Orders budget derived from ruler Legitimacy.
systems.strengths: The loop is satisfying because every choice is exclusive, priced in one currency, and has a visible countdown ('Library: 6 turns'). Opportunity cost is legible: building a granary IS not building a spearman. Staggered completion timers across cities create a natural decision cadence — you're only ever asked one question per city every few turns, but the empire aggregates into dozens of meaningful choices. Rush mechanics (whip/gold-buy/chop) convert one resource into time, which is the single most emotionally powerful conversion in strategy games — paying dearly to get the thing NOW before a war or a wonder race resolves. Old World's Orders system is the genre's best anti-micromanagement invention: it converts 'move everything every turn' into 'spend a scarce budget on what matters'.
systems.weaknesses: Civ IV whip + overflow math is a degenerate optimization mini-game (whip at 19/50 for 60 hammers, never at 20/50) that rewards spreadsheet play. One-item-at-a-time queues are absurd at scale — a modern nation builds thousands of things concurrently — and in the late game queue management across 15+ cities becomes pure tedium (the #1 complaint about Civ late game). Gold-buying trivializes production as a distinct resource once your economy snowballs. Sticker-price costs mean production is never constrained by inputs (no steel shortage can stall a Civ factory).
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT, don't adopt. At 4,600 provinces you cannot have per-province queues — that's the Civ late-game tedium multiplied 300x. Use a national/regional construction system (HoI4-style shared construction capacity allocated across projects) but STEAL Civ's presentation: every project must show a countdown, a single clear tradeoff, and a completion fanfare. Keep the rush lever but make it thematic and asymmetric: the planned economy 'whips' — Stakhanovite campaigns / forced-labor decrees that convert population welfare into immediate output with a delayed unrest cost (Civ IV slavery is literally a command-economy mechanic); the market economy 'gold-buys' — deficit spending and contractor premiums that convert money into speed with inflation cost. Cap decision count: the player should make ~1 construction decision per game-month, not per province.

systems.how_it_works: Civ V/VI: industry is a building ladder per city — Workshop → Factory → Power Plant — each a % or flat production multiplier. Civ V (and Civ VI GS) Factories/Power Plants project a REGIONAL aura: production bonus extends to all city centers within 6 tiles of the Industrial Zone, and identical regional buildings don't stack, so optimal play spaces industrial hubs to cover multiple cities. Civ VI districts make industry a map-placement puzzle: Industrial Zone adjacency bonuses from mines/quarries/aqueducts (+1 or +2 production each) reward siting factories near resource geography. Millennia goes further: improvements form transformation chains (Forester→log→Papermaker→paper→Scribe→manuscript; wheat→flour→bread), each step multiplying value (Wheat = 4 food, milled Flour = 8).
systems.strengths: The regional-aura design is quietly brilliant: it turns 'build a factory in every city' (no decision) into 'where do I place ONE industrial heartland to serve a region' (real decision), and it maps perfectly onto real geography — the Ruhr, Donbas, and Great Lakes were exactly such auras. Adjacency bonuses make industrial siting depend on resource geography, which players find deeply satisfying because the map itself argues for a plan. Millennia's chains create genuine 'economy as machine' pleasure — watching raw inputs upgrade through stages.
systems.weaknesses: Civ VI adjacency optimization becomes a solved min-max ritual (players consult placement calculators). Millennia's chain UI collapsed under its own weight — resources visible only in the city screen while building from the map, forcing constant screen-swapping; reviewers called it out as the game's biggest friction, and late-game the binding constraint degenerated into 'not enough tiles' rather than interesting scarcity. Chains that are strictly better (always mill your wheat) aren't decisions, just clicks.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the regional industrial hub with radius effects — it's the right granularity between 4,600 provinces and one national factory count. Model industry as named regional complexes (Ruhr, Urals, Manchuria) whose output serves surrounding provinces; this makes strategic bombing and territorial loss legible ('they took the Silesian complex'). ADAPT chains only at coarse grain: coal+iron→steel→machine tools/consumer goods is enough to make planned-vs-market divergence visible (Gosplan must explicitly allocate steel between tanks and tractors; the market allocates by price automatically). AVOID Millennia's error: never require the player to inspect one screen to make a decision on another — the chain state must be visible at the point of decision.

systems.how_it_works: Civ VI Gathering Storm: from the Industrial era, advanced buildings (Factory, Power Plant tiers of science/culture buildings, etc.) require Power; unpowered they still function but with yields roughly halved. Power is generated by burning stockpiled strategic resources at a flat rate — 1 Coal, 1 Oil, or 1 Uranium each → 4 Power per turn — or by renewables (hydro dams, wind/solar/geothermal) that need no fuel. Fuel choice has externalities: coal emits heavy CO2, oil moderate, nuclear minuscule, feeding the climate-change sea-level system. Nuclear Power Plants additionally carry an aging-reactor accident risk: meltdown probability rises with reactor age unless you periodically pay production for the 'Recommission Reactor' project to reset the accident timer.
systems.strengths: The genius move is soft failure: unpowered buildings degrade rather than shut off, so a power shortfall is a visible efficiency tax, not a cascade crash — players feel the pressure without a death spiral. Power creates the game's cleanest resource sink: a per-turn FLOW demand (not one-time cost) that makes coal/oil/uranium continuously scarce and therefore worth fighting over. The coal-vs-nuclear choice is a genuine tradeoff triangle (cheap+dirty vs expensive+clean+risky). The Recommission Reactor upkeep is a rare successful 'maintenance or disaster' mechanic — neglect is a real choice with tail risk.
systems.weaknesses: Arrives too late in a Civ game to matter much — by the Industrial era most games are decided, so many players ignore power entirely or slap down one plant and forget it. 4 power per fuel is flavorless arithmetic; there's no grid, no transmission, no regional blackout drama. Renewables make the whole dilemma evaporate in the late game. Meltdowns feel random-punitive to players who didn't internalize the timer.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the soft-degradation model wholesale: electricity as a national/regional flow that industry, and later computing/enrichment, consume — shortfall means all consumers run at reduced efficiency, never a hard stop. In a Cold War game power is not late-game garnish, it's the spine: enrichment plants (Oak Ridge consumed ~1% of US electricity) and heavy industry should compete for the same grid, making 'guns vs watts' a real 1950s decision. ADAPT the reactor-aging mechanic into a maintenance-culture system: rushed Soviet-style reactor programs are cheaper and faster but carry rising accident risk (Kyshtym 1957, eventually Chernobyl-class events with fallout and legitimacy damage) unless maintenance is funded — a perfect planned-economy tradeoff. Tie civilian nuclear power to the weapons program (dual-use reactors breed plutonium) so 'Atoms for Peace' is a genuine strategic choice, which Civ never does.

systems.how_it_works: All Civs: each citizen eats 2 food; surplus food fills a growth bucket whose threshold grows super-linearly with size (Civ V: ~15 + 6·(n−1) + (n−1)^1.8; Civ VI similar), so early pops arrive in 3–5 turns and late pops take 20+, an intentional soft cap. Civ IV Granary carries over half the food box after growth. Civ VI adds Housing as a second, orthogonal cap: growth −50% when 1 below the housing limit, −75% at/above it, −100% at 5 over — housing comes from water access, buildings, districts, farms. Old World: population is grown deliberately by SPENDING the Growth yield, and citizens become tile Specialists that take multiple turns to train, making each pop a placed investment. Amenities/happiness add ±10–15% growth modifiers.
systems.strengths: The food-box is one of the most legible feedback loops ever designed: surplus → visible bar → new citizen → new tile worked → more surplus. Growth as compounding investment ('farms first') teaches opportunity cost better than any tutorial. Housing is a good second constraint because it's infrastructure-shaped: you can have food and still be capped by sanitation/housing, which is historically true and creates a different build answer. The superlinear threshold elegantly prevents runaway snowballing without hard caps.
systems.weaknesses: Utterly ahistorical demography: population only grows, never ages, never has cohorts; war deaths are invisible; a size-20 city and size-3 city have the same birth behavior. Growth micro (avoid growth to dodge unhappiness, starve-swap citizens) is degenerate. Civ VI housing math (the −50% at one-below rule) is opaque enough that most players experience it as mysterious stalling. None of this can represent the thing that actually mattered in 1950: the USSR was missing 27 million people.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the food-box entirely — you have real 1950 census data for 4,600 provinces; honor it with cohort-lite demography (children/working-age/elderly per province, natural growth rates by development level, war losses that echo for decades as workforce gaps — the Soviet 1960s conscription trough should emerge from 1941–45 deaths). But STEAL the housing insight: make urbanization, not raw population, the industrial input — peasants must be moved/drawn to cities, and housing + food logistics (collectivization vs market agriculture!) gate the urbanization rate. That single constraint recreates the entire Soviet dilemma: squeeze the countryside to feed the cities and you get 1930s-style famine risk; don't, and industrialization stalls. Growth should be a slow strategic tide the player shapes with policy, not a per-city bar to micro.

systems.how_it_works: Civ: food is a per-city tile yield — farms/pastures worked by citizens; food is strictly local (no shipping between cities until late-game trade routes/Civ VI trade food). Fresh water, tech (Fertilizer +1 food per farm), and Civ VI farm-triangle adjacency (+1 food per 2 adjacent farms after Feudalism) upgrade yields. Millennia makes food one of nine 'Needs' satisfied 0–200%: 100% satisfaction = slow growth, 200% = fast, underfeeding = decline, and food participates in goods chains (wheat→flour→bread each step worth more). Old World ships Food as a national stockpiled resource that cities and armies draw on, tradeable on a market with drifting prices.
systems.strengths: Local food makes geography destiny — river valleys grow, tundra doesn't — and players internalize the map through it. Millennia's satisfaction band (100–200%) is smarter than a binary fed/starving: surplus quality-of-life has returns, which is very Cold War (butter as a legitimacy weapon). Old World treating food as a stockpileable, tradeable NATIONAL resource with prices is the most transferable model — it makes famine, granary policy, and food as war logistics all expressible.
systems.weaknesses: Civ's strictly local food is absurd for any era with railroads — cities starve beside neighbors with surplus. Food has no volatility: no harvest variance, no weather, no procurement problem; agriculture is a solved static optimization. Nobody models the political economy of extraction — WHO takes the grain from the peasants is the central question of 20th-century agrarian politics and no 4X touches it.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT Old World's national-stockpile-with-market model, then split it by system: market economies buy grain via price signals (surplus flows automatically, costs money, US grain becomes a diplomatic weapon — PL-480 food aid); planned economies use procurement QUOTAS set by the player — set them high and you industrialize fast but risk peasant resistance and famine (China 1959 must be a reachable failure state), set them low and cities/army go short. Add harvest variance (weather rolls by region) so the Virgin Lands campaign is a real gamble. Food self-sufficiency vs importing (Soviet 1970s grain purchases from the US!) should be a late-game humiliation mechanic for the planned side.

systems.how_it_works: Civ IV/V: binary/counted access — one connected Iron enables all iron units (IV), or each Aluminum unit is consumed by one unit alive (V, freed on death). Civ VI GS switched to flow-and-stockpile: each mine yields ~3/turn into a national stockpile capped at 50–100 (+10 per military building), units cost ~20 to build AND late-era units burn 1 fuel/turn as upkeep; power plants burn coal/oil/uranium per turn. Luxuries are separate: each type gives amenities/happiness to a limited number of cities, and duplicate copies are worthless domestically — existing purely to trade.
systems.strengths: GS's flow model is the best resource design in the series: it creates war-sustainment logic (you can start a tank war you can't finish), makes resource-denial bombing/blockade meaningful, and makes stockpiling before a war a real preparatory act. 'Duplicates are only good for trade' is an elegant forced-interdependence generator — it manufactures reasons to deal with rivals. Fuel upkeep per turn means oil is a continuous strategic vulnerability, exactly right.
systems.weaknesses: Stockpile caps (50–100) are gamey and tiny; the numbers are abstract tokens with no tonnage feel. Resources are binary-located (a tile has Oil or not) with no depletion, no discovery arc, no grades. The market for resources is bilateral haggling with AI, not a price system, so scarcity never shows up as cost inflation. Civ V's rigid unit-count model made resources a hard wall rather than a pressure.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT flow + stockpile + per-tick consumption as the core resource grammar — it's proven and it IS Cold War logic (SPR, rubber stockpiles, oil embargoes). Extend it with what Civ lacks: a WORLD PRICE for each commodity that responds to global supply/demand, because that's precisely where your planned-vs-market asymmetry lives — market economies buy shortfalls at world price (vulnerable to embargo and price shocks, 1973-style), planned economies barter within their bloc at fixed prices (insulated but inefficient, Comecon-style). Add discovery (1950s Middle East oil isn't fully mapped) and depletion for drama. Uranium deserves special treatment: ore → enrichment capacity → weapons/fuel as a chain, so uranium diplomacy (Congo, Czechoslovakia) matters.

systems.how_it_works: Civ I–V: the Manhattan Project is a one-time race — in Civ II/III one civ builds the wonder and it unlocks nukes for ALL civs (mutual proliferation as flavor); Civ V made it a per-civ national project (each civ must build its own, no shared unlock), typically ~750 production, after which Atomic Bombs/Nuclear Missiles are buildable units each consuming Uranium. Civ VI GS: Manhattan Project is a repeatable-prereq city project (~1000 production) unlocking the 'Build Nuclear Device' project — each device costs production plus 10 Uranium from the stockpile; Operation Ivy (another 1000-production project, needs Nuclear Fusion) unlocks thermonuclear devices with bigger blast/range. Devices are a count in a WMD inventory, delivered by bombers, missile silos, subs; no maintenance cost in VI (Civ V nukes consumed uranium supply while extant).
systems.strengths: Framing the bomb as a PROJECT with a big sticker price — not a unit — is correct and creates the wonder-race tension players remember: seeing 'a rival has completed the Manhattan Project' is one of gaming's great dread notifications. Two-tier fission→fusion (Manhattan→Ivy) gives the arms race a second act. Tying device production to a scarce uranium stockpile makes counterproliferation (deny the resource) a strategy. The project being visible-but-private creates genuine intelligence anxiety.
systems.weaknesses: It's a one-and-done: after the race there's no program — no test needed (no Trinity moment, no detection by rivals' seismographs), no yield development, no delivery-system race distinct from warheads, no arsenal maintenance/tritium decay, no secrecy or espionage dimension (in reality the Soviet program was accelerated years by spying on Manhattan — Civ has literally nothing here). AI uses nukes poorly or never, so deterrence doesn't exist as a system, only as player self-restraint. Nukes arrive when the game is decided, so the whole apparatus is vestigial.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is YOUR centerpiece — adapt aggressively. Keep the multi-stage project structure (fission device → deliverable weapon → thermonuclear → miniaturization) with big price tags, but make each stage a PROGRAM with facilities (reactors, enrichment — consuming your power grid), scientists (a stealable/defectable asset), and a mandatory TEST that rivals detect (seismic/atmospheric detection = the intelligence event Civ never fires). Make espionage a first-class accelerator: stolen program-progress should be the single biggest espionage payoff in the game, recreating Fuchs/Rosenberg. Separate warheads from delivery (bombers→IRBMs→ICBMs→SLBMs) so the missile race is its own competition. And unlike Civ, the game must remain interesting AFTER both sides have the bomb — arsenal size, survivability, and readiness feed your brinkmanship pillar; Civ's fatal flaw is that its nuclear age is an epilogue, yours is the whole game.

systems.how_it_works: Civ VI policy cards: a slotted hand of economic/military/diplomatic modifiers (+100% production toward industrial buildings, etc.) swappable at each civic, letting players 'legislate' a temporary economic focus. Millennia: National Spirits and a nine-Needs satisfaction economy where the player explicitly routes goods through conversion chains and can convert regional Production into other yields via projects — the closest any 4X gets to a planning board. Old World: the Orders economy (a per-turn action budget from ruler Legitimacy) plus stockpiled tradeable resources (food/iron/stone/wood with drifting market prices) and direct yield-purchasing — you can BUY a building's cost in stone rather than queue it.
systems.strengths: Policy cards prove players love periodic re-planning: swap-your-cards moments are mini five-year-plan reviews, cheap to execute, high agency. Old World's market prices show even a minimal price system (prices drift with your buying/selling) adds enormous texture for near-zero player burden. The Orders budget demonstrates that capping ACTIONS, not just resources, is how you keep a big empire playable — attention itself becomes the strategic resource.
systems.weaknesses: Civ cards are modifiers, not plans — nothing can fail, overshoot, or misallocate; there is no such thing as a shortage caused by your own planning error. Millennia's routing is real planning but drowned in UI friction and, being symmetric for all players, says nothing about SYSTEMS of economy. No 4X makes planned and market economies rule-distinct: everyone is the same dirigiste god-planner with different bonuses.
systems.lesson_for_1950: Your headline differentiator — build it as asymmetric INTERFACES to the same underlying economy. Planned: the player literally writes the Five-Year Plan — a periodic (real-time-paused ceremonial moment, like a Civ card-swap but weightier) allocation of steel/labor/power across sectors with targets; over- and under-fulfillment have consequences, and falsified reporting by regional officials (an espionage-adjacent internal-information problem) makes your own statistics unreliable. Market: the player does NOT allocate — firms respond to prices; the player only sets interest rates, taxes, tariffs, defense contracts, and must tolerate recessions the planner never has (but gets efficiency and innovation the planner can't buy). Adopt Old World's lesson to keep both playable: budget the player's ATTENTION — a planned-economy player should touch the economy deeply but rarely (plan reviews), a market player lightly but continuously (rate/budget nudges). Same simulation, two genuinely different games — that's the promise no 4X has kept.

systems.how_it_works: Civ IV: per-city happy/health caps from buildings, luxuries, civics; unhappy citizens stop working. Civ V: a single GLOBAL happiness pool — each city −3, each citizen −1, luxuries +4 each (first copy only); below 0, growth −75% and settler production blocked; below −10, army combat penalties and rebel spawns. Civ VI: back to LOCAL Amenities per city — 1 amenity per 2 population starting at 3; sourced from luxuries (each luxury supplies 4 cities, 1 amenity each, auto-distributed), entertainment districts, policies; happiness tiers give ±% growth (+10%/−15%) and yield modifiers, with rebellion/free-cities/loyalty loss at the extremes.
systems.strengths: Happiness as a growth-and-output throttle (not a game-over) is the right consequence shape. Civ V's global pool, whatever its flaws, made expansion itself a costed decision — the only 4X happiness system that actually restrained players. Civ VI's 'each luxury serves only 4 cities, duplicates worthless' is an elegant scarcity-and-trade generator. Loyalty/free-cities (VI) showed unhappy border regions defecting to the culturally dominant neighbor — a mechanic practically designed for Cold War influence warfare.
systems.weaknesses: Civ V's global pool created the wide-vs-tall meta distortion: unhappiness was global but the buildings fighting it were local, so 4-city Tradition 'tall' play dominated for years — a cautionary tale about one aggregate number driving degenerate strategy. Happiness sources are ahistorical shopping lists (ivory, whales); there is no consumer-goods economy, no rising expectations, no comparison with the neighbor's living standard — the actual engine of 1980s bloc collapse.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT into 'Standard of Living' as a per-province RELATIVE measure: satisfaction depends not on absolute consumer-goods supply but on trajectory (better than 5 years ago?) and on visible comparison with the other bloc (West Berlin as a shop window; radio/TV penetration imports expectations — this hooks directly into your influence-warfare pillar). Planned economies can force-suppress consumption for investment (guns over butter) at accumulating legitimacy cost that erupts in crises (1953 Berlin, 1956 Hungary, 1980 Gdansk as emergent events); market economies must fund consumption via growth or face elections. Steal Civ VI loyalty wholesale: provinces with collapsed relative living standards drift toward the other bloc's influence — that is the Cold War win condition in miniature.

key_takeaways: Civ's build-loop is satisfying because of presentation, not simulation: one exclusive choice at a time, priced in one currency, with a visible countdown and a completion payoff. At 4,600 provinces you must aggregate construction to national/regional level (Old World's Orders budget proves capping player ATTENTION is the scaling tool), but every project should still render as a Civ-style card with a timer and a tradeoff — keep total construction decisions to roughly one per game-month.

Civ VI Gathering Storm's power system is the single most transferable mechanic set: per-turn resource FLOW into stockpiles, buildings that softly degrade (~50% yields) when underpowered rather than shutting off, and reactors whose accident risk grows unless maintenance is paid.
