Adopt all three verbatim — soft degradation prevents death spirals, flow consumption makes blockade/bombing meaningful, and 'cheap rushed reactors vs funded maintenance' is a ready-made planned-economy tradeoff ending in Kyshtym/Chernobyl.

Civ's Manhattan Project proves a nuclear program should be a multi-stage PROJECT race with dread notifications, but Civ treats the nuclear age as an epilogue and has no test-detection, no espionage acceleration, no delivery race, and no functioning deterrence. Your game inverts this: fission→test(detected!)→thermonuclear→miniaturization→delivery-systems as visible-but-private programs, with stolen program-progress as the highest espionage payoff in the game — the arms race must stay interesting AFTER both sides have the bomb.

Civ IV's Slavery whip and Civ V/VI gold-buying are secretly the two economic systems your game is about: converting population welfare into immediate output (command) vs converting money into speed (market). Make them the signature asymmetric rush levers — and heed the whip's lesson that lump-sum conversion math invites degenerate timing exploits; keep conversions continuous or event-based, not overflow-optimizable.

Civ V's global happiness pool is the genre's canonical warning: one aggregate number with globally-applied costs but locally-purchased remedies produced a years-long degenerate meta (tall Tradition dominance). Keep welfare/legitimacy per-province and RELATIVE (trajectory + comparison with the rival bloc), and steal Civ VI loyalty so provinces with collapsing relative living standards drift toward the other side — that turns quality-of-life into your influence-warfare battleground instead of a maintenance chore.

No 4X has ever made planned and market economies rule-distinct — Millennia's goods chains and Civ's policy cards are symmetric planner toys, and Millennia's UI (deciding on one screen with data trapped on another) shows how chain economies die in practice. The open goal for your game: one underlying commodity simulation (flows, stockpiles, world prices) with two asymmetric interfaces — the planner writes periodic quota plans that can misallocate and be falsely reported; the market player only steers prices/taxes/contracts and must tolerate recessions. Different failure modes, different cadence of attention, same world.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris 2.2+: planets have District slots capped by planet size (a size-16 planet holds 16 districts) and Building slots unlocked by city districts/tech/pop count. Everything is built from a per-planet queue with mineral costs and build times of months-to-years game time; districts come in four generic flavors (city/generator/mining/agriculture, later industrial). Construction consumes a stock (minerals) and then imposes a permanent flow cost (energy upkeep, typically 1-2 energy per district/building) — every build decision is a stock-to-negative-flow conversion.
systems.strengths: The slot cap makes construction a real allocation decision (opportunity cost per slot), not just 'build everything eventually.' Upkeep-on-everything means expansion is never free — over-building generators/labs can bankrupt you, which players find genuinely strategic. The stock-cost/flow-upkeep pattern is the single cleanest anti-snowball device in the game.
systems.weaknesses: With 20-50+ planets, per-planet queues become click-hell; Stellaris' sector automation was notoriously non-functional at 2.2 launch ('window dressing' per forum consensus). Slots also flatten geography — a slot is a slot, so planets feel interchangeable. Queue management is tedium, not decision-making.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: keep the two-part cost (capital stock to build, ongoing flow to operate — every factory should burn coal/electricity/labor forever). But with 4,600 provinces, NEVER expose per-province build queues as the primary interface. Make the atomic decision regional/national (a Five-Year-Plan allocation, a state budget line) and let provinces receive construction algorithmically — with the planned economy doing this by explicit quota (player writes the plan) and the market economy doing it by private investment responding to prices (player shapes incentives, doesn't place buildings). That asymmetry IS your economic-systems-competition pillar.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris industry is a short production chain: miners produce minerals; metallurgists convert minerals→alloys (3.x: 6 minerals → 3 alloys per job) and artisans convert minerals→consumer goods (6→6); alloys build ships/stations, consumer goods pay pop living standards. Industrial districts provide these jobs; planetary 'designations' (Forge World, Factory World) give +% output and steer automation. Growth in industry = more pops working more jobs, multiplied by stacking % modifiers (techs, civics, repeatable techs at +5% each).
systems.strengths: The two-tier mineral→alloy chain creates a real guns-vs-butter dial (alloys vs consumer goods from the same mineral base) that players immediately understand. Designations give planets identity and specialization payoff. Chains beat raw currencies for narrative: you can SEE why your war machine starved (mineral shortfall upstream).
systems.weaknesses: Only ~2 links deep, so the chain is trivially solvable; the real optimization is modifier-stacking, which produces classic mudflation — late-game empires output 10-50x early-game numbers and the values stop meaning anything (Koster's item/currency devaluation in single-player form). Percentage bonuses stack multiplicatively into degenerate 'tall forge world' builds.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT: use a chain of 3-4 links (coal/ore → steel → machine tools/goods → capital formation), which is deep enough for shortage cascades but shallow enough to read at a glance. AVOID stacking percentage modifiers as the main progression verb — mudflation is real even in single-player; prefer step-change tech (a new production method à la Victoria 3: open-hearth → basic-oxygen steel) over +5% repeatables, so 1950 numbers still mean something in 1980. Guns-vs-butter must be the same physical input contested by military and civilian sectors, not two separate currencies.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris makes energy credits BOTH the electricity analog (upkeep for every building, district, ship, station) AND the universal money: the internal/galactic market trades every resource for energy at prices floating 20%-500% of base with a ~30% market fee, prices drifting back toward base monthly. Technicians produce it as a job output like any other resource. There are no grids, no locality — energy is a single empire-wide pool.
systems.strengths: One fungible pool is supremely legible: a single number tells you if the empire is solvent. Making 'power' the currency elegantly merges budget and infrastructure. The market gives it a floating exchange rate, so energy surpluses are always useful — no dead stockpiles.
systems.weaknesses: Because energy is money, blackouts don't exist — you can't model a grid failure, only bankruptcy. Deficit spirals are the notorious failure mode: lose one producer planet and cascading upkeep shortfalls take 'several years of pausing and hundreds of clicks' to fix (community post-mortems). Conflating currency with a physical utility erases the most interesting property of electricity: it's a non-storable FLOW with locality.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID Stellaris' conflation. Electricity in 1950 should be a non-storable, regionally-bounded flow: generation capacity (coal/hydro, later nuclear) vs regional demand, with brownouts throttling factory output in that grid region rather than draining a treasury. Nuclear power then becomes a strategic choice with character — huge capital cost, slow build, prestige and dual-use (plutonium production) implications — instead of a better technician. Keep money separate: rubles/dollars for the market bloc, and for the planned bloc money should matter LESS than material balances, which is itself a differentiating rule.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris' pop system went through three eras. 2.2: discrete pops each working one job, linear growth. 3.0: logistic growth — monthly growth points fill a 'growth required' bucket whose size scales with TOTAL empire population (required = 100 + scaling × empire pops), an explicit anti-snowball/anti-lag brake; planet-level logistic curve peaks at half carrying capacity, total capped at 5.0 pops/month. 4.0 (2025): pops abstracted into workforce units of 100, with jobs producing per-100-workforce, precisely because thousands of individual pop objects destroyed late-game performance. Pops have strata (worker/specialist/elite) with different consumer-goods upkeep and political power.
systems.strengths: Pops as the universal denominator — every building is only as good as the people staffing it — is the best idea in the game and maps perfectly onto a 1950 game with real province populations. Strata with different upkeep and political weight ties economy to politics. The logistic curve produces believable S-curves and rewards opening new land/planets.
systems.weaknesses: The 3.0 empire-wide growth cap was widely damned as illogical ('why do colonists on planet A breed slower because planet B is full?') — a mechanical brake with no fictional justification. Discrete pop objects at scale caused both lag and micromanagement (resettlement clicking). Growth was also too gameable via assembly/migration stacking.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the pop-as-denominator principle wholeheartedly — you already have real 1950 populations, your crown jewel. But learn from the 4.0 retreat: with 4,600 provinces, populations must be continuous quantities (cohorts/workforce shares per province), never discrete objects. Use real demography (birth/death rates, urbanization, the actual post-war baby boom and demographic transition) as your growth model — you don't need an artificial empire-wide brake because 30 years of real demography IS naturally bounded. Strata → classes (rural/urban worker/educated) with different consumption baskets and political weight feeds your influence-warfare pillar for free.

systems.how_it_works: Food in Stellaris is a flat per-pop upkeep (1 food/organic pop, modified by living standards) produced by farmer jobs in agriculture districts; surplus does almost nothing (minor growth bonus), deficit triggers empire-wide starvation penalties (pop growth collapse, happiness malus) and forced market purchases. Food is fully fungible and teleports empire-wide.
systems.strengths: Dead simple to read; the deficit penalty creates one clear responsibility. Trading food surpluses on the market for energy gives agrarian empires an economic identity.
systems.weaknesses: Food is a solved, boring system — players build N farm worlds early and never think about it again; surplus is nearly worthless, so agriculture has no interesting decisions after minute 30. No spoilage, no logistics, no regional famine, no farm-labor-vs-factory-labor tension.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT heavily: in 1950 agriculture is THE central planning drama — collectivization, the Virgin Lands campaign, the Great Leap famine, US grain surpluses as Cold War soft power (PL-480 food aid). Food must be regional (province-level production vs consumption with transport constraints) so famines are possible and localized, and the rural→urban labor transfer must be the core industrialization tradeoff: you industrialize exactly as fast as you can squeeze labor and surplus grain out of the countryside. Make procurement policy (forced quotas vs market prices for grain) a planned-vs-market differentiator with famine risk on one side and budget cost on the other. Surplus food should be a foreign-policy weapon, not a dead number.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris runs ~9 core resources (energy, minerals, food, alloys, consumer goods, 3 sciences, unity) plus rare strategic resources (exotic gases, crystals, motes) that gate advanced buildings/components and are found in specific systems. All are empire-wide fungible pools — no logistics, no location once extracted. The internal market converts anything to anything through energy at floating prices (20%-500% band, ~30% fee), which is a soft-landing valve for shortages.
systems.strengths: The strategic-resource layer creates map-driven scarcity and casus belli — wars fought over the only motes deposit in range are emergent geopolitics. The market band with fees is well-tuned: it rescues you from small deficits but punishes using it as a primary strategy, and bulk purchases moving the price against you elegantly caps exploitation.
systems.weaknesses: Empire-wide pooling means blockades and interdiction barely matter — the economy has no arteries to cut. Nine-plus mostly-independent currencies produce dashboard management rather than tradeoffs; several (unity) are pure abstraction. The market makes autarky vs trade a non-decision since everyone has market access.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the small-set-of-strategic-resources idea (oil, coal, steel, uranium, rubber, grain — roughly HoI4's count, ~6-8) with hard map locality — uranium in the Congo/Czechoslovakia/Colorado must MATTER. But AVOID the frictionless empire pool: resources should move along real trade routes that embargo, blockade, and COCOM-style export controls can sever — that's how economic warfare becomes a playable Cold War verb. Give the two blocs different market access: capitalist countries trade at world prices; the socialist bloc barters through Comecon at negotiated prices — the same resource layer, two different rule sets.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris has no direct analog, but its megastructure/special-project pattern is the closest lesson: giant undertakings gated by prerequisite tech + an explicit commitment (ascension perk), built in named multi-stage phases over decades, each stage costing enormous alloy stocks and a dedicated construction ship, with visible partial states on the map. Contrast with its ordinary tech: invisible points accumulating toward a card draw.
systems.strengths: Multi-stage megaprojects are Stellaris' best 'program' fiction — players narrate their Dyson sphere. Stage gating creates anticipation and intermediate strategic vulnerability (a half-built structure is a target). The up-front commitment (perk slot) makes it a strategic identity choice, not a default.
systems.weaknesses: Ordinary Stellaris research is the anti-model for a Manhattan Project: passive, abstract point-flows with no personnel, no facilities, no intelligence footprint, no failure risk. Megastructures are also pure sinks — nothing contests or observes them, so rivals can't react until completion.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the megastructure pattern into the bomb program: a named multi-stage project (reactor → enrichment/plutonium path choice → device → test → weaponization → thermonuclear) where each stage consumes concrete flows — fissile material from specific facilities (tying into your electricity/nuclear system), scarce scientist pops, and money — and each stage has an espionage-visible footprint (test detection, physicist recruitment) feeding your espionage pillar. Progress should be visible-but-uncertain to rivals, creating the historical intelligence-estimate drama ('when will they get it?'). Never model it as a research slider; it's a supply chain with a security clearance.

systems.how_it_works: Stellaris' planning layer is thin: planetary designations (+% and automation hints), sector/planet automation (historically broken — at 2.2 launch it did essentially nothing), and empire-wide edicts/policies toggling modifiers. Every empire, hive mind or megacorp, ultimately plays the same command economy where the player IS Gosplan, placing every building. The design literature frames the alternatives: Dormans/Machinations — model any economy as sources, drains, converters, and traders, and tune by classifying feedback loops (positive loops = snowball, negative loops = rubber-band); Koster — every currency needs matched faucets and drains or you get mudflation; Victoria 3 — buildings are shells you plug workforce and production methods into, with autonomous agents (pops, private investment) responding to prices; Offworld Trading Company — remove unit micro entirely and let a live market BE the gameplay.
systems.strengths: Direct command is legible and empowering at small scale — players love authoring an economy. Designations show that even weak specialization tools give planets identity. The literature's key positive: OTC proves a price system alone can carry an entire strategy game; Victoria 3 proves autonomous economic agents can coexist with player direction.
systems.weaknesses: Stellaris proves the failure mode: command-everything collapses into micromanagement the moment scale grows, and automation bolted on afterward never earns trust ('the tools to micro are bad'). Conversely, Victoria 3's launch showed fully price-driven economies can feel unaccountable and exploitable (its forums' 'fundamentally broken economics' threads). Neither game makes the CHOICE of economic system a mechanic — it's always one system.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is your game's thesis, so build it deliberately: planned economies = the player sets quantities (output quotas, investment allocations by sector/region) and the system solves for shortages — failure mode is misallocation, queues, and famine, with black markets as the emergent negative feedback; market economies = the player sets parameters (taxes, tariffs, interest rates, subsidies) and autonomous firms/consumers solve for quantities — failure mode is recessions, unemployment, and inequality feeding your influence war. Same underlying stock-flow simulation (design it in Machinations terms first: identify every source, drain, converter, and loop), two different player verb sets. And take Stellaris' hardest lesson: at 4,600 provinces, the PLANNED player must also work through aggregate instruments — even Gosplan didn't place individual factories; the plan interface is the game, not a province build menu.

key_takeaways: Pops are the universal denominator — steal this, not the implementation. Stellaris' deepest idea is that every economic output is (people × workplace × method), and its 4.0 retreat from discrete pop objects to continuous workforce proves the implementation rule: with 4,600 real-population provinces, model population as continuous cohorts with real demography (baby boom, urbanization, demographic transition), never as objects. Real demography also replaces Stellaris' hated artificial growth brakes with a naturally bounded curve.

Every asset must convert a stock cost into a permanent flow cost. Stellaris' upkeep-on-everything (build with minerals, pay energy forever) is its best anti-snowball device and the core of Koster's faucet-drain law: any resource without matched drains mudflates. Corollary: make progression come from step-change production methods (Victoria 3 style), not stacking +5% modifiers — modifier inflation is single-player mudflation and it will make your 1980 numbers meaningless.

Do not let electricity be money (Stellaris' central conflation). Power should be a non-storable, regional flow where shortfall throttles local industry (brownouts), not a treasury drain — this is what makes nuclear power a characterful investment and gives grids strategic geography. Keep currency separate, and make money itself matter differently per bloc: hard budget constraint for market economies, material balances for planned ones.

The planned-vs-market pillar has a precise mechanical formulation: planned player sets QUANTITIES and the sim solves prices/shortages (failure = misallocation, queues, famine, black markets); market player sets PARAMETERS (taxes, rates, tariffs) and autonomous agents set quantities (failure = recession, unemployment, inequality). One shared stock-flow simulation, two disjoint verb sets and failure modes. Stellaris shows what happens if you skip this: everyone plays Gosplan and drowns in micro; OTC and Victoria 3 together prove both halves are individually viable.

Locality is what Stellaris threw away and what a Cold War game cannot live without. Empire-wide fungible pools make blockades, embargoes, and export controls meaningless; route resources (uranium, oil, grain) through severable trade links and regional balances so economic warfare, COCOM lists, and food-aid diplomacy become real verbs. Stellaris' floating-price market band (20%-500%, fees, price impact from bulk buys) is still worth copying as the capitalist bloc's soft-landing valve — just deny the socialist bloc that valve and give it Comecon barter instead.

Model the bomb as a supply chain with an intelligence footprint, not a research slider. Stellaris' megastructures (staged, visible, resource-hungry, pre-committed) are the right template: reactor → enrichment path choice → test → thermonuclear, each stage consuming fissile-material flows from specific facilities and scarce scientist pops, each stage partially observable to rival espionage — so the historical 'when will they get it?' estimate drama emerges from the economy itself.
